From him this philosophy first shone out, holy and secret, as if set up in sacred temples and in their inner shrines. It was unknown to many of those who entered these holy places. Then, at set periods of time, it came out into the light as far as it could, through certain true priests, men who lived a life in keeping with the tradition of such mysteries. And it seems to me that the whole place became bright, and that visions of divine sights showed themselves everywhere.

flags.taylor: capable of enjoying it for a time
flags.why: Taylor's "for a time" is unclear: it can be read as "for a while", or as "in time", that is, to souls who live in time. The modern version takes the second reading, which fits the contrast with the gods; the Greek is not yet on the site to settle it.

notes: "One man" is Plato, as Taylor's footnote says. The "true mysteries" and their "visions" are the language of the Phaedrus (250b-c), where the soul, before birth, was initiated into the most blessed of mysteries and saw whole and steady visions.

paragraphs.modern: These are the interpreters of Plato's vision of the mysteries (the epopteia, the highest stage of initiation), who have unfolded for us the most sacred accounts of divine things and were given a nature like their leader's. I would name them as the Egyptian Plotinus; those who received the teaching from him, I mean Amelius and Porphyry; and in the third place those who grew from these like statues of heroes, Iamblichus and Theodorus; and any others who came after them, followed this divine choir, and worked at Plato's teachings with a mind inspired by the gods. From these came the man who, after the gods, has been our guide to everything beautiful and good. He received in his soul, undefiled, the most genuine and pure light of truth. He made us share in all the rest of Plato's philosophy. He passed on to us the secret teaching he had received from those older than himself. And he made us, together with him, stirred by the gods over the sacred truth about divine things.
notes: The man who "after the gods" was Proclus' guide is his teacher Syrianus, head of the school at Athens before him, as Taylor's footnote says. Theodorus is Theodorus of Asine, a pupil of Porphyry and Iamblichus.

paragraphs.modern: If we tried to give this man thanks equal to the good we have received from him, the whole of time would not be enough. But it is needful not only that we have received from others the surpassing good of Plato's philosophy. We must also leave to those who come after us a record of the blessed sights that we have seen and, as far as we could, followed, under the most perfect leader of our time, a man who reached the summit of philosophy. So perhaps we will do well to call on the gods to kindle the light of truth in our soul, and to pray to the attendants and servants of the higher beings to guide our intellect and lead it to the complete, divine and lofty end of Plato's teaching. For I think that anyone who has even the least share of intelligence will always begin what he does from the gods, and most of all when he explains the gods. We cannot understand the divine nature in any other way than by being perfected in the gods' light. Nor can we make it known to others unless the gods guide us, keeping us free of the many shapes of opinion and of the shifting variety of words, and keeping the meaning of the divine names whole. Knowing this, and following the advice of Plato's Timaeus, we first set the gods as the leaders of the teaching about themselves. May they hear our prayers and be kind to us. May they come to us gently, guide the intellect of our soul, and lead it around Plato's Hestia, the hearth at the centre of his teaching, and up to the steep heights of this inquiry. When we arrive there, we will receive the whole truth about them, and our labour to bring forth our thoughts about divine things will reach its best end: wanting to know something about them, asking others about them, and at the same time, as far as we can, searching them out ourselves.

flags.taylor: lead it about the Vesta of Plato
flags.why: Taylor gives Hestia her Latin name, Vesta. She is the goddess of the hearth, who in the Phaedrus (247a) stays at home while the other gods go round; Proclus means the fixed centre of Plato's teaching, round which the soul is led.

notes: The Timaeus (27c) says that everyone with the least good sense calls on a god before any undertaking, small or great; Timaeus then prays before his account of the universe. Taylor's footnote: the Greek lacks the word "only" in "not only that we have received".

paragraphs.modern: So much for the preface. Next I must explain the method of the teaching I propose, what one should expect it to be, and what preparation its hearer should bring, so that he is ready to approach, not my words, but Plato's philosophy, which lifts up the intellect and makes us like the gods. For the fitness of the hearers should match the kind of teaching. It is as in the mysteries. Those skilled in such things first prepare vessels to receive the gods. To bring the gods to be present, they do not use just any lifeless things, or any animals, or any men. Out of each kind they bring into the sacred rites only what is naturally able to share in divine light.
notes: The "vessels" are the statues and other objects that the theurgists prepared to receive the presence of a god.

paragraphs.modern: First, then, I will divide this discourse into three parts. At the beginning I will look at all the common teachings about the gods that Plato gives in summary, and at the power and the high standing of the axioms of theology wherever they appear. In the middle of the work I will study the whole orders of the gods, count their distinctive characters, mark out their processions as Plato does, and refer everything to the principles laid down by the theologians. At the end I will speak about the gods praised here and there in Plato's writings, whether they are above the world or in the world, and I will refer what is taught about them to the whole classes of the divine orders.
notes: The three parts are Book I (the common teachings), Books II-VI (the orders of the gods, from the One down to the gods in the world), and a third part on particular gods, which is lost or was never written; Taylor's own seventh book stands in for it.

paragraphs.modern: In every part of this work, too, we will prefer what is clear, distinct and simple to their opposites. What is handed down through symbols we will turn into clear teaching. What is handed down through images we will carry back to the patterns they copy. What is written more as plain statement we will test by reasoning from causes. What is set out by demonstration we will examine, and we will also explain the kind of truth it holds and make it known to the hearers. What is put in riddles we will make clear from elsewhere, not from other people's assumptions, but from Plato's most genuine writings. And of the things the hearers meet at once, we will consider how they agree with the things themselves. From all this, one complete form of Plato's theology will appear to us: its truth, which runs through all of divine thought; the one intellect that gave birth to all the beauty of this theology; and the sacred unfolding of this vision. Such, as I have said, will be the present work.

The hearer of these teachings is supposed to be adorned with the moral virtues. He should have bound, by the rule of virtue, every mean and unharmonious motion of the soul, and tuned them all to the single form of the practical wisdom that belongs to intellect. For, as Socrates says, it is not lawful for the impure to touch the pure. Every bad person is wholly impure, and the opposite kind of person is pure. He should also have been trained in all the methods of logic, and have studied many sound ways of analysis and many of division, and their opposites, in keeping, I think, with Parmenides' advice to Socrates. For until one has gone through such a contest of arguments, the knowledge of the divine kinds, and of the truth set in them, is hard to reach and hard to enter. Third, he must not be untrained in the study of nature. Whoever has become familiar with the many opinions of the natural philosophers, and has explored in a way, in images, the causes of the things that are, will more easily go on to the nature of the separate and first beings. So, as I have said, the hearer of this work must not be ignorant of the truth found in appearances, nor a stranger to the paths of learning and the mathematical studies they contain, for through these we gain a less bodily knowledge of divine being. But all of these must be bound together under intellect, which leads. He must also share in Plato's dialectic, and practise the immaterial activities that are separate from bodily powers. He must long to contemplate true beings by intellectual insight joined with reason. Then let him give himself wholly to explaining the divine and blessed teachings, and fill his soul, as the Oracle says, with deep love. For, as Plato says somewhere, to grasp this vision no better helper than love can be found.

flags.taylor: intelligence in conjunction with reason [true] beings
flags.why: Taylor adds "true" in brackets, and his footnote corrects the Greek he translated (from "intelligence with reason" as a subject to "by intelligence with reason"). The phrase is the Timaeus' (28a): what always is, is grasped "by intellectual insight together with a rational account".

notes: "It is not lawful for the impure to touch the pure" is Socrates in the Phaedo (67b). Parmenides advises the young Socrates to train himself in the method of hypothesis before he speaks of the Forms (Parmenides 135c-136c). The Oracle is one of the Chaldean Oracles, which bid the soul fill itself with "deep love". Plato says that for this possession human nature could find no better helper than love in the Symposium (212b).

paragraphs.modern: He must also be trained in the truth that runs through all things, and wake his intelligible eye, the eye of intellect, to what is real and complete truth. He must settle himself in a firm, unshaken and safe kind of divine knowledge. He must be persuaded to admire nothing else, and not even to turn his attention to other things, but to hurry towards divine light with a fearless activity of reasoning and with the power of a tireless life. In short, he must set before himself the kind of activity and rest proper to one who means to be such a leader of the choir as Socrates describes in the Theaetetus. Such, then, is the size of our task, and such the method of our discourses on it. But before I begin to set out what I have proposed, I want to speak about theology itself, its different kinds, and which forms of theology Plato approves and which he rejects. Once these are known, we will more easily learn, in what follows, what supports the demonstrations themselves.
notes: The "leader of the choir" (coryphaeus) is the true philosopher of the Theaetetus' digression (173c-174a), who does not know the way to the market place, but whose mind ranges over the whole of nature.

paragraphs.modern: Everyone who has ever touched on theology has called the things that are first by nature "gods", and has said that the science of theology is about them. Some have held that bodily being is the only thing that exists at all. They have put every kind of bodiless nature second to it in being, taken the principles of things to be bodily in form, and shown that the state in us by which we know these principles is bodily too. Others make all bodies depend on bodiless natures, and place the first hyparxis in soul and its powers. These, I think, call the best of souls "gods", and they call the science that reaches as far as these souls, and knows them, "theology". Still others bring the many souls out of another, older principle, and set intellect as the leader of all things. These say that the best end is the union of the soul with intellect, and they think the life of intellect the most honourable of all things. No doubt they also take theology and the study of intellectual being to be one and the same. All these, then, as I have said, call the first and most self-sufficient principles of things "gods", and the science of them "theology".
notes: Taylor's footnote: hyparxis is "the summit of any nature, or blossom, as it were, of its being", its first and highest mode of existence. The Workshop keeps the word.

paragraphs.modern: But Plato's account of the divine, and his alone, rejects every bodily nature as a principle. Everything that can be divided and has extension cannot by nature make or keep itself in being. It has its being, its activity and its being acted on through soul and the motions soul contains. Plato shows that the being of soul is older than bodies, but depends in turn on an intellectual reality. For whatever is moved in time, even if it moves itself, is of a more ruling nature than what is moved by another, but comes after an eternal motion. So he shows, as we have said, that intellect is the father and cause of bodies and souls, and that everything whose life is spent in changes and unfoldings both exists and acts around intellect.
notes: Plato shows that soul, the self-moving motion, is older than bodies in the Laws (X 896a-c) and the Phaedrus (245c-e), and that soul depends on intellect in the Timaeus (30b) and the Philebus (30c).

paragraphs.modern: Plato, however, goes on to another principle, wholly set apart from intellect, more bodiless and more inexpressible, from which all things, even the very last, must have their existence. For not all things are by nature fit to share in soul, but only those that have some life in them, clearer or dimmer. Nor can all things enjoy intellect and being, but only those that exist according to Form. But the principle of all things must be shared by all things, if it is to leave nothing out, since it is the cause of everything that in any way is said to be. Plato found by divine insight this first principle of all things, which is higher than intellect and hidden in places no one can reach. He showed three causes, or monads, and showed that they are above bodies: soul, the first intellect, and a union above intellect. From these, as from monads, he brings out their own numbers: one multitude made of unities, a second made of intellects, and a third made of souls. For every monad leads a multitude of its own rank. And as Plato joins bodies to souls, so he joins souls to intellectual Forms, and these again to the henads of beings. But he turns all things back to one unshared unity. Once he has run back as far as this unity, he holds that he has reached the highest end of the study of all things, and that this is the truth about the gods: the truth that is about the henads of beings, and teaches their processions and their distinctive characters, how beings are in contact with them, and the orders of Forms that depend on these unitary realities.

flags.taylor: one multitude indeed being uniform
flags.why: Taylor's "uniform" (Greek henoeides, "one-like") does not mean "all the same": it means having the form of the One, made of unities. The first multitude is that of the henads, the gods.

notes: Taylor's two footnotes on this paragraph: "unical" means "characterized by unity", and "unity" here (the henads) means "of the nature of the One". The Workshop renders Taylor's "unities" as "henads", and his "unical" as "unitary".

paragraphs.modern: Plato teaches us that the study of intellect, and of the Forms and kinds that turn about intellect, comes after the science of the gods themselves. The study of intellect grasps the intelligibles, and the Forms that the soul can know through the outward-reaching activity of intellect. But the science of theology goes beyond this. It is about the secret and inexpressible hyparxeis of the gods, and it traces how they are set apart from each other and how they come to light from the one cause of all. So I believe that the intellectual part of the soul can grasp the intellectual Forms and the difference among them. But the summit of intellect, its "flower", as they say, and its hyparxis, is joined to the henads of beings, and through these to the hidden union of all the divine henads. For though we have many powers of knowing, it is through this alone that we are by nature able to be joined to that hidden union and to share in it. The race of the gods cannot be grasped by sense, since it is set above all bodies. Nor by opinion and discursive reason, for these are divided and deal with things of many forms. Nor by intellectual insight joined with reason, for that kind of knowledge belongs to true beings. But the hyparxis of the gods rides upon beings, and is marked out by the very union of all things. So it follows, if the divine nature can be known in any way at all, that it must be grasped by the hyparxis of the soul, and known through it as far as possible. For we say that everywhere like is known by like: the perceptible by sense, what is opined by opinion, what is reasoned by discursive reason, and the intelligible by intellect. So the most unitary nature must be known by the one in us, and the inexpressible by what is inexpressible in us.
notes: Taylor's footnotes: dianoia, here "discursive reason", is "the discursive activity of reason, or the power of the soul that reasons scientifically"; "the doxastic" is the object of opinion. "The flower of intellect" is the Chaldean Oracles' phrase. The hyparxis of the gods "rides upon" beings as the gods in the Phaedrus (247b-c) ride in their chariots on the back of the heaven.

paragraphs.modern: Socrates rightly says in the First Alcibiades that the soul, when it enters into itself, will see all other things, and god himself. For as it bends towards its own unity, the centre of all life, and lays aside multitude and the variety of the many powers it holds, it climbs to the highest look-out over all beings. In the holiest of the mysteries, they say, the initiates first meet the many kinds of many shapes that are hurled out in front of the gods. But when they enter the inside of the temple, unmoved and guarded by the rites, they truly receive divine light into themselves, and, stripped of their clothes, as they would say, they share in the divine nature. The same thing, I think, happens in the vision of all things. When the soul looks at what comes after it, it sees the shadows and images of beings. But when it turns back to itself, it unfolds its own being and the reason-forms it holds. At first it sees, as it were, only itself. But when it goes deeper into the knowledge of itself, it finds in itself both intellect and the orders of beings. And when it goes into its inmost part, the inner shrine, as it were, of the soul, it sees, with its eyes closed, the race of the gods and the henads of beings. For all things are in us in the manner of soul, and so we are by nature able to know all things, by waking the powers and images of the whole that we hold.

flags.taylor: the multiform, and many-shaped genera, which are hurled forth before the Gods
flags.why: Taylor's footnote says these are "evil daemons". They are the frightening apparitions that, in the rites, appear before the god appears; the modern version keeps Proclus' image.

notes: The First Alcibiades (132c-133c): the soul that looks into the best part of itself, where wisdom is, will know god and itself. "With its eyes closed" recalls the initiate (mystes) of the mysteries, whose name Proclus' readers took from "closing" (myein) the eyes.

paragraphs.modern: And this is the best use of our activity: to reach out to the divine nature itself, with our powers at rest; to circle around it in harmony; to wake all the multitude of the soul to this union; and, laying aside everything that comes after the One, to settle ourselves in, and be joined to, what is inexpressible and beyond all things. For the soul may climb until it ends its flight in the principle of things. When it has arrived there and seen the place there, it may come down from it and make its way through beings, unfolding the many Forms, searching out their monads and their numbers, and grasping by intellect how each depends on its own henad. Then we may hold that the soul has the most perfect science of divine natures, seeing as one the processions of the gods into beings, and the distinctions of beings around the gods. Such, then, by Plato's judgement, is our theologian. And theology is a state of this kind: it unfolds the very hyparxis of the gods; it sets apart and contemplates their unknowable and unitary light, distinct from the character of the things that share in them; and it makes it known to those worthy of this activity, which is blessed and holds all things together at once.
notes: "The place there" is the place beyond the heaven of the Phaedrus (247c), which the gods and the best souls see.

paragraphs.modern: After this complete account of the first part of our inquiry, we must set out the ways in which Plato teaches us the sacred ideas about divine natures. For he does not seem to have taught about them in the same way everywhere. Sometimes he unfolds the truth about them by an activity inspired by the gods, and at other times dialectically. Sometimes he announces their inexpressible characters in symbols, and at other times he goes back up to them from images and finds in them the first causes of all things. In the Phaedrus, inspired by the Nymphs, and having exchanged human understanding for something better, divine madness, he reveals with an inspired voice many secret teachings about the intellectual gods, and many about the liberated rulers of the universe, who lead the many gods of the world upward to the monads that are intelligible and separate from the wholes of the world. And speaking still more of the gods to whom the world is allotted, he praises their acts of thinking, their making of the world, their pure providence and their governing of souls, and everything else that Socrates says in that dialogue in an inspired way, as he plainly says himself, laying this madness to the gods of the place.

flags.taylor: the liberated rulers of the universe
flags.why: "Liberated" (Greek apolytoi, "unbound") is Proclus' name for an order of gods between the gods above the world and those in it: they rule the world but are not bound to it. The Workshop keeps Taylor's word.

notes: In the Phaedrus Socrates says he is "possessed by the Nymphs" (238c-d, 241e) and blames "the gods of the place" (262d); his second speech tells of the gods' procession round the heaven (246e-247c).

paragraphs.modern: In the Sophist, arguing dialectically about being and about how the One is set apart from beings, and raising difficulties against those older than himself, he shows how all beings depend on their cause and on the first being. Being itself shares in the unity that is set above all things. It is a one that has unity as something it undergoes, but not the One itself: it is subject to the One and united to it, but it is not what is first of all one. In the same way, in the Parmenides, he unfolds dialectically, through the first hypotheses, the processions of being from the One and the One's transcendence, and does so, as he says in that dialogue, by the most perfect division of this method. Again, in the Gorgias he tells the myth of the three Craftsmen and of their allotment as makers of the world. This is not only a myth but a true account. In the Symposium he speaks of the union brought by Love. And in the Protagoras he speaks of how the mortal animals were given their shares by the gods. In these he hides the truth about divine natures in symbols, and unfolds his mind only so far as to hint at it to the most genuine of his hearers.

flags.taylor: that it is a passive one
flags.why: Taylor's "passive one" renders the Sophist's phrase (245a): being "has unity as an affection", has the one as something that happens to it. It does not mean that being is inactive; the modern version says what is meant.

notes: The Sophist (244b-245e) argues against those before Plato who said that all is one. The "three Craftsmen" of the Gorgias (523a) are Zeus, Poseidon and Pluto (Hades), who divide the realm of Kronos, as in the Iliad (15.187-193). Aristophanes' speech in the Symposium (189c-193d) and Diotima's (201d-212a) speak of love that unites; the Protagoras' myth (320c-322a) tells how Epimetheus and Prometheus gave the animals their powers.

paragraphs.modern: Then there is the teaching given through the mathematical studies, and the treatment of divine things drawn from ethical or physical discussions, of which much can be found in the Timaeus, much in the dialogue called the Statesman, and much scattered in other dialogues. If you like, I will mention these too. Here also, for those of you who want to know divine things through images, the method will be plain. For all these give a shadowy picture of the powers of the divine. The Statesman, for example, pictures the making of the world in the heavens. The shapes of the five elements, given in geometrical proportions in the Timaeus, show in images the distinctive characters of the gods who ride on the parts of the universe. And the divisions of the being of soul in that dialogue give a shadowy picture of the whole orders of the gods.
notes: The Statesman's myth of the world's two motions (269c-274e); the five regular solids of the Timaeus (53c-56c); the division of the world-soul by numbers (35a-36d). Taylor's footnote: the words "in the Timaeus" are missing from the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: I pass over the fact that Plato composes constitutions, likening them to divine natures and to the whole world, and orders them from the powers the world holds. Through the likeness of mortal things to divine ones, all of these show us in images the processions, orders and works of making of the divine natures. These, then, are the ways of teaching about the gods that Plato uses.
notes: The constitutions are those of the Republic and the Laws; the Republic's city is "a pattern laid up in heaven" (592b).

paragraphs.modern: It is clear from what has been said that there must be just this many of them. Those who treat divine things by hints either speak in symbols and myths, or through images. Of those who state their thoughts openly, some build their accounts by science, and others by inspiration from the gods. Whoever wants to point to divine things through symbols is Orphic, and in short agrees with those who write myths about the gods. Whoever does it through images is Pythagorean. For the Pythagoreans invented the mathematical studies to help recollect divine things, which they try to reach through these, as through images. According to the witness of their historians, they refer both numbers and shapes to the gods. The inspired person, who unfolds the truth about the gods by itself under divine inspiration, stands most clearly among the highest of the initiators. These do not think it right to show the divine orders or their characters to their companions through veils, but announce the gods' powers and numbers because the gods themselves move them. But to hand down divine things by science is the glorious distinction of Plato's philosophy. For Plato alone, I think, of all those known to us, has tried to divide by method, and set in order, the regular procession of the divine kinds, how they differ from each other, the characters common to the whole orders, and the characters given out to each one. The truth of this will be clear when we give the proper demonstrations about the Parmenides and all the divisions it contains.

flags.taylor: when we frame precedaneous demonstrations
flags.why: Taylor's "precedaneous" (an old word for "going first, principal") means the demonstrations that belong first and properly to the subject: the account of the Parmenides, which is the core of the work.

paragraphs.modern: For now we will note that Plato does not accept all the inventions of poetry and drama, but only those that point to the beautiful and the good and do not clash with divine being. The way of myth, which points to divine things by guesswork, is ancient. It hides the truth under many veils, and works much as nature does, which holds out perceptible inventions in place of intelligible things, material in place of immaterial, divisible in place of indivisible, and images, things that have a false being, in place of what is wholly true. But Plato rejects the more tragic way of making myths used by the old poets. They wanted to set up a secret theology about the gods, and for this they invented wanderings, cuttings, battles, tearings apart, rapes and adulteries of the gods, and many other symbols of the truth about the divine that this theology hides. This way Plato rejects, and he says that it is in every way most foreign to education. But he holds that those myths about the gods are more convincing, and closer to the truth and to the philosophic temper, which say that the divine is the cause of all good and of no evil, that it does not change at all, always keeping its own order unchanged, and that it holds in itself the source of truth but is never the cause of any deceit for others. Such are the patterns of theology that Socrates gives in the Republic.
notes: Republic II-III (377b-392c): Socrates rejects Hesiod's and Homer's stories of Kronos' deeds and the gods' battles, and lays down the "patterns of theology" (379a): god is the cause only of good things (379b-c), does not change (380d-381e), and does not deceive (382a-383a).

paragraphs.modern: So all of Plato's myths, while keeping the truth hidden, do not have even an outward dress that clashes with our untaught and unspoiled sense of the gods. They carry an image of the way the world is put together, in which the visible beauty is worthy of the divine, and a beauty more divine than this is set in the unseen lives and powers of the gods. This, then, is one of the ways of myth about divine things: it passes from what seems lawless, irrational and disordered into order and limit, and aims at putting together the beautiful and the good.

But there is another way, which he teaches in the Phaedrus. It consists in always keeping the myths of theology unmixed with accounts of nature, and in taking care never to confuse theology and the study of nature with each other, or to swap one for the other. For as divine being is separate from the whole of nature, it is right that accounts of the gods should also be clean of physical explanations. Such a mixing, he says, is laborious, and to make the things that happen in nature the meaning of a myth is the work of no very good man: for example, someone who, by his supposed wisdom, takes the Chimaera, the Gorgon and the like to be natural events. Socrates in the Phaedrus disapproves of this way of handling myths, and makes its followers say, in a story, that Orithyia playing with the wind Boreas and thrown down the rocks means nothing more than that Orithyia, a mortal girl, was carried off by Boreas out of love. For it seems to me that the hidden meaning of myths about the gods should always be holier than the apparent one. So if anyone gives us physical interpretations of Plato's myths, about the things below the moon, we must say that they wholly miss the philosopher's aim. Only those interpretations truly explain the truth these myths hold which aim at a divine, immaterial and separate reality, and which, looking to it, build and take apart the myths in keeping with our inborn sense of divine things.
notes: Phaedrus 229c-230a: Socrates will not explain away the myth of Boreas and Orithyia as a girl blown off the rocks by the north wind, since then one would have to explain Centaurs, the Chimaera, Gorgons and Pegasus too, "a laborious task, and not for a very lucky man". Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek.

paragraphs.modern: Now that we have counted all these ways of Plato's theology, and shown what building and taking apart of myths fits the truth about the gods, let us next consider where, and from which dialogues above all, we think Plato's teachings about the gods can be gathered, and by looking for which patterns or forms we can tell his genuine writings from the false works that are put down to him.

The truth about the gods runs, one may say, through all of Plato's dialogues. In all of them thoughts of the first philosophy are sown, holy, clear and above nature: in some more dimly, in others more plainly. These thoughts stir those who can in any way share in them towards the immaterial and separate being of the gods. In each part of the universe, and in nature herself, the Craftsman of all that the world holds set up likenesses of the unknowable hyparxis of the gods, so that all things might turn back to the divine nature through their kinship with it. In the same way, I believe, Plato's divine intellect weaves thoughts about the gods into all his writings, and leaves nothing without mention of the divine, so that from the whole of them a recollection of all things may be gained and given to the genuine lovers of divine things.

But if I must set before the reader, out of many, the dialogues that above all unfold for us the sacred teaching about the gods, I would not be wrong to count among them the Phaedo and the Phaedrus, the Symposium and the Philebus, and with these the Sophist and the Statesman, the Cratylus and the Timaeus. All these are full, through and through, one may say, of Plato's divine science. In the second rank after these I would put the myth in the Gorgias and the one in the Protagoras; also what is said in the Laws about the gods' providence, and what is taught about the Fates, or the mother of the Fates, or the turnings of the universe, in the tenth book of the Republic. In the third rank you may, if you like, put those Letters through which we can reach the science of divine natures. For in them the three kings are mentioned, and very many other divine teachings worthy of Plato's vision are given. So we must look to these, and search out in them each order of the gods.
notes: The Laws on providence: Book X (899d-905d). The Fates and their mother, Necessity, and the turning spindle of the universe: the myth of Er, Republic X (616b-617d). The "three kings" are in the Second Letter (312e): "all things are about the king of all ... the second about the second, and the third about the third".

paragraphs.modern: So from the Philebus we can receive the science of the one Good and of the two first principles of things, together with the triad that comes to light from them. You will find all of these set out clearly by Plato in that dialogue. From the Timaeus you can gain the study of the intelligibles, a divine account of the monad of the Craftsman, and the fullest truth about the gods of the world. From the Phaedrus, a scientific knowledge of all the intelligible and intellectual kinds, and of the liberated orders of gods, which are set just above the circuits of the heavens. From the Statesman, the study of the making of the world in the heavens, of the uneven periods of the universe, and of the intellectual causes of those periods. From the Sophist, the whole of becoming below the moon, and the distinctive character of the gods to whom the region below the moon is allotted, who preside over its comings to be and passings away. And about each of the gods we can find many ideas fit for sacred things in the Symposium, many in the Cratylus, and many in the Phaedo. For in each of these dialogues the divine names are mentioned, more or less, and from these it is easy for those trained in divine things to find out, by reasoning, the distinctive character of each.

flags.taylor: the two first principles of things, together with the triad
flags.why: Taylor's footnote: the Greek he translated lacks the word "triad". The two principles are limit and the unlimited (Philebus 16c, 23c), and the triad is the mixture and its cause; Proclus treats them in Book III.

notes: The Phaedrus' place "above the heaven" and the gods' procession (246e-247e); the Statesman's two periods of the universe (269c-270a).

paragraphs.modern: But we must show that each teaching agrees with Plato's principles and with the sacred traditions of the theologians. For all Greek theology is the offspring of the sacred tradition of Orpheus. Pythagoras first learnt the rites of the gods from Aglaophemus, and Plato, second, received a complete science of the gods from the writings of the Pythagoreans and the Orphics. For in the Philebus, referring the study of the two kinds of principles, limit and the unlimited, to the Pythagoreans, he calls them men who live with the gods and are truly blessed. Philolaus the Pythagorean left us in writing many wonderful thoughts about these principles, praising their common procession into beings and the separate work of making that each performs. In the Timaeus, when Plato means to teach us about the gods below the moon and their order, he turns to the theologians, calls them the sons of the gods, and makes them the fathers of the truth about these gods. And at last he gives the orders of the gods below the moon as coming from the wholes, following the procession of the intellectual kings that they teach. Again, in the Cratylus he follows the theologians' traditions about the order of the divine processions. In the Gorgias he takes up Homer's teaching about the three Craftsmen. In short, wherever he speaks of the gods, he speaks in keeping with the theologians' principles. He rejects the tragic side of mythical invention, but he lays down the first principles in common with the makers of myths.

flags.taylor: Pythagoras first of all learning from Aglaophemus the orgies of the Gods
flags.why: Taylor's "orgies" means the secret rites of the gods (Greek orgia), not revelry.

notes: Philebus 16c-d: the ancients, "better than us and living nearer the gods", handed down that all things are made of one and many, with limit and the unlimited in them. Timaeus 40d-41a: of the gods below the heaven we must trust "those who spoke before, being, as they said, the offspring of the gods", who give the line Ouranos and Ge, then Okeanos and Tethys, then Phorkys, Kronos and Rhea, then Zeus and Hera. Cratylus 395e-396c and 402b-c follow the same line of names. The three Craftsmen: Gorgias 523a, from the Iliad (15.187-193).

paragraphs.modern: But perhaps someone will object here that we are not presenting Plato's theology properly, scattered as it is everywhere, and that we are trying to heap together different pieces from different dialogues, as if we were eager to collect many things into one mixture, instead of drawing them all from one and the same source. If that were so, we could refer different teachings to different works of Plato, but we would by no means have a proper, primary teaching about the gods. Nor would there be any dialogue that gives us the complete and whole procession of the divine kinds and how they are ranked with each other. We would be like those who try to get a whole from parts, for want of a whole that is prior to the parts, and to weave the perfect together out of imperfect things, when the imperfect ought, on the contrary, to have the first cause of its coming to be in the perfect. The Timaeus, for example, will teach us the study of the intelligible kinds, and the Phaedrus seems to give us an orderly account of the first intellectual orders. But where will we find how the intellectual is ranked with the intelligible? And how the second comes to be from the first? In short, we will not be able to show how the procession of the divine orders comes about from the one principle of all things, and how, in the generations of the gods, the orders between the One and the complete number are filled in.

Further, the objector may say, where will be the holiness of your much-praised science of divine natures? It is absurd to call these teachings Plato's when they are gathered from many places and, as you admit, brought into Plato's philosophy under names foreign to it; nor can you show one whole and complete truth about divine natures. Perhaps, they will say, certain people younger than Plato have written and left to their pupils one complete form of theology. You, then, can bring out one whole account of nature from the Timaeus, and from the Republic or the Laws the finest teachings about character, which tend to one form of philosophy. Only the work of Plato that holds all the good of the first philosophy, and may be called the summit of the whole study, you leave aside, and so you will lack the most perfect knowledge of beings, unless you are so foolish as to boast of mythical inventions, though the explaining of such things is full of the probable and empty of the demonstrative. Besides, such things are only brought into Plato's dialogues by the way. The myth in the Protagoras, for instance, is put in for the sake of the art of politics and the demonstrations about it. In the same way the myth in the Republic is put in for the sake of justice, and the one in the Gorgias for the sake of self-control. For Plato joins mythical stories to inquiries into ethical teachings not for the sake of the myths, but for the sake of the main aim: so that we may not only train the intellectual part of the soul through contending arguments, but so that the divine part of the soul may receive the knowledge of beings more perfectly, through its sympathy with more sacred things. For from other kinds of discourse we seem like people forced to accept the truth; but from myths we are moved in an inexpressible way, and we call up our unspoiled ideas, revering the sacred teaching they hold.

flags.taylor: certain persons, junior to Plato, have delivered in their writings, and left to their disciples, one perfect form of theology
flags.why: The objector's point is that later writers (it is not said who; Proclus may mean the authors of the Chaldean Oracles, or his own school) have left complete theologies, while Plato himself has not, in any one work.

notes: Taylor's footnotes correct two places in the Greek he translated ("of the gods" missing, and a word read as "ethical").

paragraphs.modern: So, I think, Timaeus rightly thinks it fitting that we should bring forth the divine kinds by following the makers of myths, as sons of the gods, and accept that they always generate the second natures from the first, even if they speak without demonstration. For this kind of discourse is not demonstrative but inspired, and the ancients invented it not from necessity but for the sake of persuasion, aiming not at mere teaching but at sympathy with the things themselves. And if you are willing to look at the causes not only of the myths but of the other teachings of theology, you will find that some are scattered in Plato's dialogues for the sake of ethical questions, and others for the sake of physical ones. In the Philebus, Plato speaks of limit and the unlimited for the sake of pleasure and of the life lived by intellect. For I think the second are kinds of the first. In the Timaeus the account of the intelligible gods is taken up for the sake of the study of nature that is proposed. So everywhere images must be known from their patterns, and the patterns of material things must be immaterial, of perceptible things intelligible, and the patterns of natural forms must be separate.

flags.taylor: For I think the latter are species of the former
flags.why: Pleasure and the life of intellect (the latter) are kinds of the unlimited and of limit (the former): in the Philebus (27e-28a, 31a) pleasure belongs to the unlimited, and intellect is kin to the cause of the mixture.

notes: Timaeus 40d-e: we must believe the sons of the gods "though they speak without probable or necessary proofs".

paragraphs.modern: Again, in the Phaedrus, Plato praises the place above the heaven, the depth below the heaven, and every kind beneath this, for the sake of the madness of love, and of how the souls' recollection comes about and their passage there from here. Everywhere, one may say, the main aim is either physical or political, and the thoughts about divine natures come in either for the sake of discovery or of perfection. How, then, can a study like yours still be holy and above nature, and worth studying above everything, when it can show neither the whole in itself, nor the perfect, nor what comes first in Plato's writings, but lacks all these, and is forced, not natural, and has an order that is not its own but brought in from outside, as in a play? Such are the objections that may be raised against our plan.
notes: The place above the heaven and the "subcelestial arch" are in the Phaedrus (247b-c); recollection and the soul's journey (249b-250c).

paragraphs.modern: To an objection of this kind I will give a fair and clear answer. I say that Plato everywhere speaks of the gods in keeping with ancient report and with the nature of things. Sometimes, for the sake of the cause of the things in hand, he carries them back to the principles of the teachings, and from there, as from a look-out, studies the nature of what is in hand. But sometimes he sets the science of theology as his main aim. In the Phaedrus his subject is intelligible beauty, and how beauty, shared from there, runs through all things; and in the Symposium it is the order of love.
notes: Phaedrus 249d-250e: the beauty seen above the heaven, and its image here; Symposium 210a-212a: the ascent to the beautiful itself.

paragraphs.modern: But if we must survey, in one dialogue of Plato's, the whole of theology, complete and connected, reaching to its full number, I may perhaps say something surprising, which only those close to us will find plain. Still, we must be bold, since we have begun on such arguments, and say against our opponents that the Parmenides, and the sacred ideas it holds, will give you all you want. For in this dialogue all the divine kinds proceed in order from the first cause and show how they are linked to and depend on each other. The highest, those akin to the One and of a first nature, are given a unitary, hidden and simple form of hyparxis. The last are multiplied, divided into many parts, and rich in number, but weaker in power than those of a higher order. The middle ones, in fitting proportion, are more composite than their causes but simpler than their own offspring. In short, all the axioms of the science of theology appear complete in this dialogue, and all the divine orders are shown linked together. So this is nothing other than the famous generation of the gods, and the procession of every kind of being from the inexpressible and unknowable cause of all things. The Parmenides, then, kindles in the lovers of Plato the whole and perfect light of the science of theology. After it, the dialogues mentioned before give out parts of the sacred teaching about the gods. All of them, one may say, share in divine wisdom and wake our own ideas about the divine nature. All the parts of this sacred teaching must be referred to these dialogues, and these again to the one complete study of the Parmenides. In this way, I think, we will make the more imperfect depend on the perfect, and the parts on the wholes, and we will show accounts made like the things they explain, as Plato's Timaeus says. Such, then, is our answer to the objection that may be raised against us. And so we refer Plato's teaching on the gods to the Parmenides, just as everyone with the least understanding agrees that the Timaeus holds the whole science of nature.

flags.taylor: the celebrated generation of the Gods
flags.why: Proclus means a theogony, an account of the gods' births such as Hesiod's and the Orphics'; the Parmenides, read by the school, gives the same in the form of a deduction.

notes: The Timaeus (29b): accounts are akin to the things they explain. The school read the hypotheses of the Parmenides' second part (137c-166c) as an account of all the orders of reality from the One down; the next chapters set out this reading.

paragraphs.modern: By this, however, I seem to have stirred up for myself a contest on two fronts against those who try to study Plato's writings. I see two kinds of people who will oppose what has been said. The first thinks it right to look for no other aim in the Parmenides than practice in arguing both sides, and not to bring into this dialogue a crowd of secret and intellectual teachings foreign to its purpose. The second kind are more serious than these, and lovers of the Forms. They say that one of the hypotheses is about the first God, another about the second God and the whole of intellectual nature, and a third about the natures after this, whether they are the higher kinds, or souls, or some other kind of beings. For to inquire into these details does not belong to the present discussion.
notes: The first group follows Parmenides' own words (135c-136c), that what follows is "an exercise". The second is the reading of Plotinus (V.1.8) and his school: the first hypothesis is about the One, the second about intellect, the third about soul. "The higher kinds" are the angels, daemons and heroes, the kinds above human souls.

paragraphs.modern: These, then, divide three of the hypotheses in this way. But they do not think it right to concern themselves with the many gods, the intelligible and intellectual kinds, the natures above the world and in the world, or to unfold all these by division and search them out with care. For according to them, though Plato speaks of intellectual beings in the second hypothesis, the nature of intellect is one, simple and undivided. Whoever holds the view of the Parmenides that we have stated must contend against both. But the contest is not equal against both. Those who make the Parmenides an exercise in logic are themselves attacked by those who hold the divine way of reading it. And those who do not unfold the many beings and the orders of divine natures are, as Homer says, in every way men to be revered and skilled. But for the sake of Plato's philosophy we must raise difficulties against them too, following in this our leader to the most holy and sacred truth. It is right also to set out, so far as it helps our aim, what we take to be the truth about the hypotheses of the Parmenides. For in this way, perhaps, by a process of reasoning, we may take in the whole of Plato's theology.
notes: "To be revered and skilled" (or "awesome"): Helen's words to Priam in the Iliad (3.172), which Socrates uses of Parmenides in the Theaetetus (183e). "Our leader" is Syrianus.

paragraphs.modern: First, then, let us look at those who drag the aim of this dialogue down from the truth of things to an exercise in logic, and see whether they can possibly agree with Plato's writings. It is clear to everyone that Parmenides means to hand on the dialectical method in earnest. With this in view he runs through it in the same way for each of the things that really are, such as sameness, difference, likeness, unlikeness, motion and remaining at rest, and he urges those who want to find the nature of each in an orderly way to take up this exercise as a great contest. He also says that it was no easy task for a man of his age. He likens himself to the horse of Ibycus, and gives every sign that this method is serious work and not a contest of mere words. How, then, can we reduce to empty arguments the ideas about which the great Parmenides composed this discourse, showing that they need serious discussion? And how is it reasonable to suppose that an old man would busy himself with contests of words, and that a lover of the truth of things would spend so much study on this method: he who thought that nothing else really is, and who had climbed to the high look-out of being itself? Whoever accepts this must suppose that Plato is mocking Parmenides in this dialogue, showing him dragged down from the soul's most intellectual visions to the contests of the young.

flags.taylor: assimilates himself to the Ibycean horse
flags.why: In the Parmenides (137a) the old Parmenides compares himself to the ageing racehorse in a poem of Ibycus, who trembles before the race because he knows what is coming; so Parmenides fears to swim "so great a sea of words".

notes: Parmenides 135c-137b: the method of supposing that each thing is and is not, for sameness, likeness, motion and the rest, which Parmenides calls "a great labour". Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: If you like, let us also consider what Parmenides promises, and on what subject he began this discussion. Was it not about being, as he taught it, and about the unity of all beings? He reached out to this, though his aim was hidden from the many, and he urges us to gather the many beings into one undivided union. If this is the one being, the highest thing, set wholly above the reasonings that belong to opinion, is it not absurd to mix teachings about intelligibles with arguments from opinion? Such a form of discourse does not suit the subject of true beings, and thinking the unseen and separate causes does not go with dialectical exercises. These differ from each other as far as intellect stands above opinion, as Timaeus tells us; and not Timaeus only, but also the daemonic Aristotle, who, speaking of a power of this kind, urges us to make our inquiries neither about things wholly hidden from us nor about things already very well known.

flags.taylor: the dæmoniacal Aristotle
flags.why: Taylor's "dæmoniacal" means "more than human, inspired": a title of honour, not of reproach. The power Aristotle speaks of is dialectic, the art of arguing from accepted opinions (Topics I, 100a-101b).

notes: The Timaeus (27d-28a, 51d-e) sets intellect, which grasps what always is, above opinion, which grasps what comes to be.

paragraphs.modern: So Parmenides, who puts the science of beings above what seems true to those who rank sense before intellect, is far from bringing knowledge by opinion to an intellectual nature, since that kind of knowledge is doubtful, varied and unsteady. Nor would he study true being with this wisdom of opinion and with empty discussion. A varied form of knowing does not fit what is simple, nor the many-formed what is one-like, nor opinion the intelligible.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects the Greek he translated (to "the form does not fit").

paragraphs.modern: Further, we must not leave out this point either: such a way of discussion is wholly foreign to Parmenides' subject. He speaks about all beings, and sets out the order of all things, their procession beginning from the One and their return ending in the One. But the method of arguing both sides is very far from the study that belongs to science. Would it not seem, then, that Plato has given Parmenides an unfitting subject, if it is said that he looks only to an exercise in opposing arguments, and stirs up this whole unrolling of reasonings for the sake of the skill the exercise trains? In fact we find that in all the other dialogues Plato gives each philosopher a subject suited to his own teaching. To Timaeus he gives the teaching about nature; to Socrates, that about the city; to the Stranger from Elea, that about being; and to the priestess Diotima, that about love. Then each of the other dialogues keeps to the arguments that suit the writings of the dialogue's main speaker. Parmenides alone would seem wise in his poems and in his careful search for true being, but on Plato's stage he would lead a childish Muse. So this view charges Plato with an unlike imitation, though he himself blames the poets for giving the sons of the gods a love of money and a life ruled by the passions. How, then, can we refer a discussion of opinions and empty arguments to the leader of the truth of beings?

flags.taylor: accuses Plato of dissimilitude of imitation
flags.why: That is, of making Parmenides speak out of character, an imitation unlike its original: the fault Plato finds in the poets (Republic III 390e-391e, Achilles and the gifts).

paragraphs.modern: But if we must leave aside many arguments and call Plato himself as a witness to the subject of this discussion, let us cite what is written in the Theaetetus and the Sophist, for from these what we say will be clear. In the Theaetetus a young man urges Socrates to refute those who say that being is unmoved, and Socrates, coming to Parmenides' view among them, gives at the same time the reason for his care. "I am more ashamed before Parmenides," he says, "who is one of these, than before all the rest. For I met him when I was very young and he was very old, and he seemed to me to have a depth that was altogether noble. So I am afraid that we may not understand what was said, and much more afraid that we fall short of what Parmenides meant." So we are right to say that the discussion before us is not about an exercise in logic, nor does it make this the end of the whole, but that it belongs to the science of the first principles of things. For how could Socrates, if Parmenides had used a skill of this kind and neglected the knowledge of things, bear witness that his discourse had a depth that was altogether noble? And what dignity could there be in taking up a method that goes by opinion through opposing arguments, and in setting out to invent such arguments?
notes: Theaetetus 183e-184a. Socrates' meeting with Parmenides is the scene of the Parmenides itself.

paragraphs.modern: Again, in the Sophist, Socrates urges the Stranger from Elea to unfold clearly what he has proposed, and shows that he was by now used to deeper discussions. "Tell me," he says, "is it your custom to go through a subject at length by yourself, when you are able to show it to someone by questions? I mean the kind of discussion Parmenides himself once used, with arguments of great beauty, which I heard when I was very young and he was very old." What reason can be given, then, for not believing Socrates when he says that Parmenides' arguments were of great beauty and had a noble depth? Why should we lower Parmenides' discussion, throw it down from being and what is, and turn it into a common, trifling and empty contest, without considering that discussions of that kind suit only the young, or regarding the subject of the being that has the character of the One, or anything else that tells against such an opinion?
notes: Sophist 217c.

paragraphs.modern: I also think that the authors of this view should consider the power of dialectic as Socrates shows it in the Republic: how, as he says, it surrounds all the studies like a coping wall; how it lifts those who use it up to the Good itself and the first henads; how it cleans the eye of the soul, settles it in true beings and in the one principle of all things, and ends at last in what is no longer a hypothesis. If the power of this dialectic is so great, and the end of this road so mighty, we must not confuse arguments from opinion with a method of this kind. The first looks to the opinions of men, while the second is called idle talk by the many. The first has no share at all in the sciences of learning; the second is their coping wall, and the way to it lies through them. Again, reasoning by opinion has as its end what appears, while the dialectical method tries to reach the One itself, always using steps of ascent for this, and at last ends beautifully in the nature of the Good.

flags.taylor: surrounds all disciplines like a defensive enclosure
flags.why: The Republic's word (534e) is a coping stone, set on top of the studies: dialectic crowns the mathematical studies as the top course of a wall.

notes: Republic VII 532a-534e: dialectic, the eye of the soul drawn out of the mire (533d), and its end in the Good; the "unhypothetical principle" (VI 510b, 511b). Dialectic called "idle talk" by the many: the Parmenides (135d), where Parmenides tells Socrates to train in what the many call idle talk. Taylor's footnote: the word "end" is missing from the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: So it is not right to drag down to arguments from opinion a method that has its place among the most exact sciences. The merely logical method, which governs imagination as it follows demonstrations, is of a second rank, and is pleased only with contentious debates. But our dialectic uses chiefly division and analysis as first sciences, imitating the procession of beings from the One and their return to it again. It also sometimes uses definitions and demonstrations, and before these the method of defining, and before that the method of dividing. The method of opinion, on the other hand, lacks the irrefutable reasonings of demonstration. Must not these powers, then, be kept apart from each other? And must not Parmenides' discussion, which uses our dialectic, be free of the empty variety of mere argument, and build its reasonings with a view to being itself and not to what appears? This is enough in answer to those who find fault with our view. For if all this cannot convince them, we would try in vain to persuade them and urge them on to the study of things.

flags.taylor: presides over the demonstrative phantasy
flags.why: Taylor's "phantasy" is imagination: the merely logical method rules the imagination that follows the steps of a proof, not intellect.

paragraphs.modern: But a greater and harder contest remains for me, against those lovers of the study of beings who look to the science of the first causes as the end set before them in the hypotheses of Plato's Parmenides. If you like, we will carry out this contest with many and better-known arguments.

First, we will mark out what our argument against them will be about, since this, I think, will make Plato's sacred teaching about divine natures as clear as it can be. There are nine hypotheses discussed by Parmenides in this dialogue, as we have shown in our commentary on it. The five that come first suppose that the One is, and through this supposition all beings, the middles of the whole and the ends of the processions of things, can be supposed to be. The four that follow bring in the One as not being, as the dialectical method directs. They show that if the One is taken away, all beings, and everything that appears to exist, must be wholly overturned, and they set out to refute this supposition. Some of the hypotheses plainly reach every conclusion by reason, but others (if I may put it so) show things more impossible than impossibilities. Some before us saw, I think, that this must happen in these hypotheses, and thought it worth discussing in their treatises on this dialogue.
notes: Proclus' Commentary on the Parmenides survives in part (to the end of the first hypothesis); the Greek of it is on the Neoplatonists' shelf. Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: As to the first of the hypotheses, almost everyone agrees that through it Plato praises the principle of all things that is beyond being, as inexpressible, unknowable and above all being. But not everyone explains the next hypothesis in the same way. The older Platonists, and those who shared in Plotinus' philosophy, say that an intellectual nature appears in this hypothesis, coming from the principle that is beyond being, and they try to fit the conclusions of this hypothesis to the one and complete power of intellect. But our leader to the truth about the gods, Plato's companion in talk (to use Homer's words), who brought what was unlimited in the theory of the older philosophers to limit, and turned the confusion of the different orders into an intellectual distinction in the writings he shared with his circle: this leader of ours, in his treatise on this subject, bids us divide the conclusions distinctly, carry this division over to the divine orders, and fit the first and simplest of what is shown to the first of beings; to suit those of the middle rank to the middle natures, by the order they have among beings; and the last and many-formed to the last processions. For the nature of being is not one, simple and undivided. Among perceptible things, the mighty heaven is one, yet holds in itself a multitude of bodies. The monad holds multitude together, but in the multitude there is an order of procession, and of perceptible things some are first, some middle and some last. And before these, among souls, from one soul there comes a multitude of souls, and some of these are set nearer to their whole and others further from it, while others fill in the middle between the extremes. In the same way, no doubt, among the wholly true beings, the one-like and hidden kinds must be set in the one and first cause of all things; others must proceed into all multitude and into a whole number; and others, in the middle, must hold the bond between them. Nor is it right to fit the characters of the first natures to the second, or those of a lower order to those more unitary. Among them some must have powers different from others, and there must be an order in this procession of true beings, and an unfolding of the second from the first.

flags.taylor: confabulator of Plato (that I may use the language of Homer)
flags.why: Homer's word (oaristes, "familiar companion in talk") is used of Minos, who "conversed with great Zeus" (Odyssey 19.179); Proclus gives it to Syrianus, as Plato's familiar.

notes: "Our leader" is Syrianus, whose commentary on the Parmenides is lost; Proclus follows it here. The view of the "older Platonists" is Plotinus' (V.1.8): the second hypothesis is about intellect.

paragraphs.modern: In short, the being that has the character of the One proceeds from the unity prior to beings, but generates the whole divine kind: the intelligible, the intellectual, that above the world, and that which proceeds as far as the order in the world. Our teacher also says that each of the conclusions points to a divine character. And though all the conclusions fit all the processions of the one being, that is, of being with the character of the One, I think it is no wonder that some conclusions agree with some orders more than with others. For what expresses the character of certain orders does not necessarily belong to all the gods, while what belongs to all is surely present, all the more, in each. So if we credit Plato with a division of the divine orders brought in from outside, and cannot show clearly that in other dialogues he praises the processions of the gods from on high to the furthest end of things, sometimes in myths about the soul and at other times in other ways of theology, we would be wrong to credit him with such a division of being, and with it of the procession of the One. But if we can show from other dialogues that he has in some way praised all the kingdoms of the gods (as will be plain in the course of this work), is it not impossible that in the most sacred of all his works he should set out, in the first hypothesis, the One's transcendence over all the kinds of beings, over being itself, the being of soul, Form and matter, and yet make no mention of the divine processions and their orderly separation? If we should study only the last things, why do we touch on the first principle before the others? If we think it right to unfold the multitude of the hypotheses, why do we pass over the kind of the gods and the divisions it holds? And if we unfold the natures between the first and last of things, why do we leave unknown the whole orders of the divine beings that lie between the One and the natures that are made divine in any way? All this shows that such an account of the whole falls short of the science of divine things.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects the Greek he translated ("orders" for "actions").

paragraphs.modern: Further, Socrates in the Philebus calls on those who love the study of beings to use the method of division, and always to search out the monads of the whole orders, and the dyads, triads, or any other numbers that proceed from them. If this is rightly laid down, then the Parmenides, which uses the whole dialectical method and speaks about the being that has the character of the One, should neither look for multitude in the One, nor stay in the one monad of beings, nor, in short, bring the whole multitude of first beings straight up to the One above all beings. It should unfold, as in the first order, the beings that are hidden and akin to the One; as in the middle rank, those kinds of gods that are in procession, more divided than the most united, but given a more perfect union than those that have proceeded furthest; and as in the last rank, those that are by the last division of powers, and with them those whose being has been made divine. So if the first of the hypotheses is about the One above all multitude, the hypothesis that follows must not unfold being itself in an unlimited and indistinct way, but must give all the orders of beings. For the method of division does not allow us to bring the whole of multitude at once up to the One, as Socrates teaches us in the Philebus.
notes: Philebus 16c-17a: we must look for one Form, then two or three or some other number, and not pass at once from the one to the unlimited.

paragraphs.modern: Besides, we can show the truth of what we say from the very method of the demonstrations. The first conclusions become plain at once from the fewest, simplest and best-known ideas, which are, as it were, common notions. Those next in order become plain through more, and more varied, ideas. And the last conclusions are the most composite of all. For he always uses the first conclusions to serve the proof of those that follow, and in the way he links these conclusions he gives us an intellectual pattern of the order kept in geometry and the other mathematical studies. So if accounts carry an image of the things they explain, and if the order of what is shown must be as the unfolding of the demonstrations is, it seems to me that what takes its start from the simplest principles must be in every way of a more primary nature, and set as joined to the One, while what is always multiplied, and depends on varied demonstrations, must have proceeded further from the existence of the One.
notes: Taylor's two footnotes correct words of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: For demonstrations that have two conclusions must hold the conclusions that come before them. But those that hold first, self-evident and simple ideas are not necessarily united with the more composite ones, which are shown through more middle terms and are further from the principle of beings. So it appears that some conclusions point to more divine orders and others to lower ones; some to more united orders and others to more multiplied ones; some to more one-like processions and others to more many-formed ones. For demonstrations always proceed from causes and from what is first. If, then, the first conclusions are the causes of the second, there is an order of causes and effects in the multitude of the conclusions. To confuse all things and study them without distinction as one agrees neither with the nature of things nor with Plato's science.

Let us, then, take up this question in another way, and see with discursive reason where anything empty is said. Let it be said, if you like, and we will grant it first, that the conclusions of this second hypothesis are about true being. But true being is a multitude, and not just one itself like the One before beings. For being has unity as something it undergoes, as the Stranger from Elea tells us in the Sophist. And our opponents themselves agree on all sides, for they set what is first as the One, intellect as one-many, soul as one and many, and body as many and one. Since, then, this has been said a thousand times, that in true being there is multitude together with union, will they say that these conclusions fit the whole of being but not its parts, or both the whole and its parts? And again we ask them: do they give all the conclusions to each part of being, or different ones to different parts?
notes: Sophist 245a-b. The ladder one, one-many, one and many, many and one is the reading of the first three hypotheses that Plotinus gives (V.1.8), applied down to bodies.

paragraphs.modern: If they think that each conclusion fits the whole of being alone, being will be made of non-beings, what is moved of unmoved things, what remains of things without rest, and in general all things will be made of their opposites. Then we will no longer agree with Parmenides' account, which says that the parts of the being that has the character of the One are in a way wholes, and that each of them is one and being, just like the whole. But if we give all the conclusions to each part, and there is nothing we do not make all things, how can the summit of being, what is most of all one, hold a wholeness and a boundless multitude of parts? How can it hold at one and the same time the whole of number, shape, motion and rest, and in short all Forms and kinds? These differ from each other, and the hypothesis will assert impossible things. Things near the One will be as multiplied as things far from it; what is first will be no less a multitude than what is last; the last will be no less one than the first; and the things in the middle will be no different, in division, from the extremes.
notes: Parmenides 142d-143a: each part of the one being has both one and being, and so is itself a whole.

paragraphs.modern: So it is not right to give all this multitude of conclusions to the whole alone, nor to see everything alike in all the parts of being. It remains that different conclusions must fit different things. Then the listing of the conclusions must be either disordered or ordered. If they say it is disordered, they speak in keeping neither with the dialectical method, nor with the way of demonstrations, which always bring second things out of first, nor with Plato's science, which always follows the order of things. If they say the conclusions are ordered, I think they must begin either from the things first by nature or from the last. If from the last, then the being that has the character of the One will be last, and what moves in time will be first. But this is impossible. For what shares in time must, far before that, share in first being; but what shares in first being need not share in time. So first being is above time. If, then, Plato begins from first being and ends with what shares in time, he proceeds from above, from the first to the last parts of true being. So the first conclusions are to be referred to the first orders, the middle ones, for the same reason, to the middle orders, and the last, plainly, to the last. For, as our argument has shown, different conclusions must be given to different things, and such a distribution must begin from the highest.
notes: The second hypothesis begins with "the one, if it is" (142b) and ends with the one that shares in time, becoming older and younger (151e-155d).

paragraphs.modern: The order of the hypotheses, too, is to my mind enough proof of what we say. For with us the One that is set apart from all multitude is given the first order, and the unfolding of all the arguments begins from it. The second order after it is about true beings and the unity they share in. And the third, next in line, is about soul. Is it about every soul, or not? We answer that our leader Syrianus has finely shown that the account of the whole souls is included in the second hypothesis. If, then, the order of these three hypotheses follows the nature of things, it is clear that the second is produced from the first and the last from the second. For I would ask those who are not wholly untrained in such discussions: what can be more akin to the One than the being that has the character of the One, which the first conclusion of the second hypothesis unfolds? Or what can be more akin to soul than what shares in time, which is divided, and is the last thing shown in this hypothesis? For the life of partial souls, as of whole souls, is in time. First being is what first shares in the One, and through its link with being it has a hyparxis that goes beyond the unshared unity. If this hypothesis is the middle one, and we fit the highest conclusions to the highest things, we should surely fit the middle to the middle. For this hypothesis begins from first being and proceeds through all the kinds after it, until it ends in a nature that shares in time.

flags.taylor: has a redundant hyparxis with respect to the imparticipable unity
flags.why: Taylor's "redundant" means "having something over": first being has, beyond the unshared One, being added to its unity; it is one-and-being, not the One alone.

notes: "Partial souls" are individual souls such as ours; "whole souls" are the souls of the world and of the heavenly bodies. The third hypothesis (155e-157b), on the one that both is and is not, Proclus takes to be about partial souls.

paragraphs.modern: Further, we can show the same things as we have said from what is agreed by the interpreters of Plato who were skilled in divine things. Plotinus, in his book On Numbers, asks whether beings are before numbers or numbers before beings, and plainly says that first being is before numbers and generates the divine number. If he is right in this, and being generates the first number, while number is produced by being, it is not right to confuse the order of these kinds, or gather them into one reality, or, since Plato brings out first being separately and number separately, refer each of the conclusions to the same order. For it is in no way lawful for a cause and its effect to have either the same power or the same order. They are distinct from each other, the science of them is distinct too, and their nature and their definition are not one and the same.
notes: Plotinus, Ennead VI.6, On Numbers (chapters 8-9): being is prior to number, and being in its unity generates number. In the Parmenides, number comes after the one being (143a-144a).

paragraphs.modern: After Plotinus, Porphyry, in his treatise On Principles, shows by many fine arguments that intellect is eternal, but holds in itself something prior to the eternal, through which it is joined to the One. For the One is above all eternity, while the eternal has the second, or rather the third, rank in intellect. It seems to me necessary that eternity be set in the middle between what is prior to the eternal and the eternal. But of this later. All the same, this much can be gathered from what has been said: intellect holds in itself something better than the eternal. Granting this, we ask the father of this view whether this something better than the eternal is only the being that has the character of the One, or is also whole and parts, all multitude, number and shape, what is moved and what remains at rest; or whether we are to give some of the conclusions to it and not others. All these cannot fit a nature prior to eternity, since every intellectual motion, and rest too, is set in eternity. But if we are to give some of the conclusions to it and not others, it is clear that we must look for other orders in intellect, and refer each conclusion to the order it seems best suited to. For intellect is not one in number and indivisible like an atom, as it seemed to some of the ancients, but holds in itself the whole procession of first being.
