notes: Porphyry's On Principles is lost; this is one of the few reports of it. "Eternity in the middle" is the Timaeus' "eternity remaining in one" (37d), which Proclus sets between being and the eternal living being.

paragraphs.modern: Third after these, the divine Iamblichus helps our case. In his treatise On the Gods he blames those who place the kinds of being among the intelligibles, because their number and variety are further from the One. Then he tells us where they should be placed: they are produced at the end of the intellectual order, by the gods there. How the kinds of being both are and are not among the intelligibles will be made clear later. But if, in his arrangement of the divine orders, the intelligibles are set above the kinds of being, much more are they above likeness and unlikeness, equality and inequality. So each conclusion should not be fitted alike to everything, so as to refer them to the whole breadth of the intelligible or the intellectual order. So, from what the best of the interpreters have said when they philosophized by their own teachings, both the multitude of the divine orders and that of Plato's arguments are to be seen as proceeding by an orderly distinction.
notes: Iamblichus' On the Gods is lost. The "kinds of being" are the Sophist's greatest kinds (254b-255e): being, rest, motion, sameness and difference.

paragraphs.modern: In addition to what has been said, this too can be stated: on no other view can we find a reasoned answer to the many difficulties that arise here, and we would ignorantly credit this work of Plato's with what is rash and empty. First, why are there just so many conclusions, neither more nor fewer? There are fourteen. But we cannot give the reason why there are so many unless we distribute them together with the things themselves. Second, we will not be able to find why the conclusions are ordered as they are, some placed before and others after by the reason of science, unless the order of the conclusions follows the procession of beings. Third, why are some conclusions known from what was proved just before, and others from earlier proofs? That the One is a whole and has parts is proved from the being that has the character of the One; but that it is in itself and in another is placed next after having a shape, yet is proved from whole and parts. Or why are some things often proved from two of the points shown before, and others from one? We will be ignorant of each of these, and unable to study their number, their order or their kinship by science, unless we follow the things themselves and show that this whole hypothesis is a dialectical arrangement, proceeding from on high through all the middle kinds down to the end of first being.
notes: The Parmenides (144e-145b): the one being is a whole with parts, then has shape, then is in itself and in another (145b-e), proved from whole and parts.

paragraphs.modern: Again, if we say that all the conclusions prove only by syllogism, how will we differ from those who say that this whole discussion is made of arguments from opinion and is only a contest of words? But if it proves not only by syllogism but by demonstration, then the middle term must be the cause of the conclusion and prior to it by nature. Since, then, we make the conclusions of the earlier reasonings the middle terms of those that follow, the things the arguments are about must have a like order in being. What they produce must be the causes of what lies below them and generate what is second. If this is granted, how can we allow that all of them have the same character and nature? For a cause and what is produced by a cause are set apart from each other.
notes: Aristotle, Posterior Analytics I.2 (71b): demonstration is a syllogism from premises that are prior to the conclusion and its causes.

paragraphs.modern: Those who say that one nature is to be looked for in all the arguments will also fail to see how, in the first three conclusions, the One remains unseparated from being, and is first separated in the fourth, while in all the conclusions that follow the One is looked at as being by itself. Must not these orders, then, differ from each other? For what is without separation, being hidden and undivided, is more akin to the One, while what is separated has proceeded further from the first principle of things.

Again, if you will consider the multitude of the arguments and the length of the hypothesis, how much it differs from the one that follows it, from this too it will not seem to you to be wholly about one unseparated nature. For reasonings about divine things are drawn together in the higher causes, because in these the hidden is more than the plain, and the inexpressible more than the known. But they become many and are unfolded as they go on to divine orders nearer to our nature. For what is more akin to the inexpressible, the unknowable and what is set apart in places no one can reach, has a hyparxis further from being put into words. But what has proceeded further is better known to us, and plainer to the imagination, than what exists before it.

This, then, being fully proved, the second hypothesis must unfold all the divine orders. It must proceed from on high, from the simplest and most unitary, to the whole multitude, all the number of divine natures, in which the order of true being ends. This true being is spread beneath the henads of the gods, and is at the same time divided together with their hidden and inexpressible characters. If we are not mistaken in granting this, it follows that from this hypothesis we must take the continuity of the divine orders, the procession of the second from the first, and the distinctive character of all the divine kinds. Their communion with each other, their distinction proceeding by measure, and the helps that may be found in other dialogues on the truth of real beings or the henads they hold: all are to be referred to this hypothesis. For here we may contemplate the whole processions of the gods and their complete orders, by the science of theology. Since we have already shown that the whole work of the Parmenides looks to the truth of things, and was not devised as an empty unrolling of words, the nine hypotheses it discusses, using the dialectical method but studying with divine science, must be about things and certain natures, either middle or last. If Parmenides admits that his whole discourse will be about the One, and how it stands with respect to itself and all other things, it is clear that the study of the One must begin from the highest and end in the last of all things. For the hyparxis of the One proceeds from on high as far as the dimmest reality of things.
notes: Parmenides 136b-c, 137b: Parmenides will speak "about the one itself", what follows for it and for the others if it is and if it is not.

paragraphs.modern: The first hypothesis shows by negations the inexpressible transcendence of the first principle of things, and shows that it is set apart from all being and all knowledge. So the next hypothesis, as nearest to it, must clearly unfold the whole order of the gods. For Parmenides takes up through the whole of this hypothesis not only the intellectual character of the gods and the character that belongs to their being, but also the divine mark of their hyparxis. For what other one can be shared by being than the one that is in every being divine, and through which all things are joined to the unshared One? As bodies are joined to soul through their life, and as souls reach out through their intellectual part to the whole intellect and the first act of thinking, so true beings, through the one they hold, are led back to a union set apart, and remain in union with this first cause without going out from it.

flags.taylor: subsist in unproceeding union with this first cause
flags.why: Taylor's "unproceeding" means "without going forth": though true beings proceed from the One, through the one in them they also remain in it.

paragraphs.modern: But this hypothesis begins from the one being, the being that has the character of the One, sets the summit of the intelligibles as the first after the One, ends in a being that shares in time, and brings the divine souls down to the last of the divine orders. So the third hypothesis must show, by its varied conclusions, the whole multitude of partial souls and the differences among them. And this is how far the separate and bodiless reality proceeds.

After this comes the nature that is divided about bodies and cannot be separated from matter, which the fourth hypothesis gives, as hanging from the gods above. The last is the coming forth of matter, whether taken as one or as many, which the fifth hypothesis shows by negations, through its unlike likeness to the first. But sometimes the negations are privations, and sometimes they are the causes set above all that is produced. And most wonderful of all, the highest negations only deny, but some of them by transcendence and others by lack. Each of the hypotheses after these affirms, the one as a pattern and the other as an image. The middle hypothesis answers to the order of soul, for it is made of affirmative and negative conclusions, but it has negations ranked together with its affirmations. Nor is it simply multiplied, as material natures are, nor does it have a one brought in from outside. The one it holds, though still one, is in motion and multiplication, and in its processions is, as it were, swallowed up by being. These are the hypotheses that unfold all beings, both separable and inseparable, together with the causes of all things, both those set apart and those in things themselves, by the hyparxis of the One.

flags.taylor: the highest negations are only enunciative, but some in a supereminent manner, and others according to deficiency
flags.why: The first hypothesis denies everything of the One because the One is above it all; the fifth denies everything of matter because matter falls short of it all. Taylor's "enunciative" means simply denying, without affirming anything else. Taylor's footnotes correct the Greek he translated in two places of this paragraph ("likeness" for "unlikeness").

notes: The fourth hypothesis (157b-159b) is about "the others" when the one is, taken as forms in matter; the fifth (159b-160b) about "the others" with no share in the one, taken as matter.

paragraphs.modern: But there are four other hypotheses beside these. By taking away the One they show that all things must be wholly overturned, both beings and things that come to be, and that no being could any longer exist. This is so that he may show the One to be the cause of being and of keeping in being: that through it all things share in the nature of being, and each has its hyparxis hanging from the One. In short, through all beings we gather by reasoning that if the One is, all things are, down to the last reality, and if it is not, nothing is. The One, then, is the cause that makes all things exist and keeps them; and Parmenides himself draws this conclusion at the end of the dialogue. But we have treated fully, in our commentaries on that dialogue, the hypotheses of the Parmenides, their division and the study of their parts, so that a long discussion of these points here would be superfluous. Since from what has been said it is clear where we may take the whole of theology from, and from which dialogues we may gather into one the theology given out in parts, we will next treat of Plato's common teachings, which are fitted to sacred things and reach to all the divine orders, and show that each of them is defined by him with the most perfect science. For common things come before peculiar ones, and are better known by nature.
notes: The last words of the Parmenides (166c): "if the one is not, nothing is."

paragraphs.modern: First, then, we will take up what is proved in the Laws, and see how it leads the way in the truth about the gods and is the oldest of all the other sacred ideas about the divine nature. Plato asserts three things in this work: that there are gods; that their providence reaches to all things; and that they govern all things by justice and are not turned aside by anything worse.
notes: Laws X (885b, 907b): there are three errors about the gods, that they do not exist, that they do not care for men, and that they can be won over by prayers and sacrifices. Book X answers all three.

paragraphs.modern: It is plain that these hold first place among all the teachings of theology. For what can lead more than the hyparxis of the gods, their providence, which has the form of the good, and their unchanging and unswerving power? Through these the gods produce what is second to them in a one-like way, keep themselves undefiled, and turn what they produce back to themselves. The gods govern other things but are not acted on by what is below them, and they do not change with the variety of the things their providence reaches. We will learn how these things are defined by nature if we try to take in, by reasoning, Plato's scientific method about each of them; and before these, if we look at the irrefutable arguments by which he proves that there are gods, and then consider the questions linked with this teaching.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated ("more ancient").

paragraphs.modern: Of all beings, then, some must only move, others must only be moved, and those between must both move and be moved. Of these last, some must move others while being moved by others, and others must move themselves. These four realities, too, must be set in order one after another. What is only moved, and is acted on, depends on other causes before it. What moves others and is moved by another comes before it. What moves itself is above what moves and is moved: it begins from itself, and through its own motion gives other things the appearance of being moved. And what is unmoved comes before everything that shares in motion, whether in producing it or in undergoing it. For everything that moves itself has its perfection in passage and in an extension of life, and so depends on another, older cause, which is always the same and in the same way, and whose life is not in time but in eternity. For time is an image of eternity.
notes: Laws X 893b-895b: the ten kinds of motion, among which the motion that moves itself and others is first. "Time is an image of eternity": Timaeus 37d.

paragraphs.modern: So if everything moved by itself is moved in time, while the eternal form of motion is above what is carried along in time, the self-moving nature will be second in order, and not the first of beings. What moves others and is moved by others must depend on a self-moving nature: and not this alone, but every production that is moved by another, as the Athenian Stranger shows. For if all things stood still, he says, and there were no self-moving natures among things, there would be nothing that is first moved. What is unmoved is not by nature fit to be moved, so there would then be no first moved; and what is moved by another needs another power to move it. Only the self-moving nature, then, beginning from its own activity, will move both itself and, in a second way, others. Such a thing gives the power of being moved to the natures moved by others, just as an unmoved nature gives the power of moving to all beings. Third, what is only moved must first depend on what is moved by another but moves others. For the other things, and the series of moved things that stretches in order from on high to the last, must be filled with their own middle terms.
notes: Laws X 895a-b: if all things came to a standstill, the first motion to arise would be the self-moving one.

paragraphs.modern: So all bodies belong among the things that by nature are only moved and are acted on. For they produce nothing, since they have an extended existence and share in size and bulk; and everything that produces and moves others produces and moves by using a bodiless power.

Of bodiless natures, some are divided about bodies, while others are set above such division about the last of things. The bodiless things divided about the bulk of bodies, whether they are qualities or forms in matter, are among those moved by another while moving others. Because they have a bodiless lot, they share in the power of moving. But because they are divided about bodies, they lack the power of turning towards themselves, are divided along with what underlies them, and are filled with sluggishness from it. So they need a moving nature that is not carried in a seat foreign to it but has its existence in itself. Where, then, shall we find what moves itself? Things stretched out into natures with bulk and extension, or divided in them and inseparable from them, must either be only moved or move through others. But, as we said before, a self-moving nature must come before these, set wholly in itself and not in others, and fixing its activities in itself and not in things other than itself. So there is a certain other nature, set apart from bodies, both in the heavens and in these changeable elements, from which bodies first get the power of being moved. If we must find what this kind of being is (rightly following Socrates, and looking to the end of things), which by its presence gives to the natures moved by others an appearance of self-motion, to which of the natures mentioned shall we give the power by which things are moved from themselves? All lifeless things are only moved by another, and whatever they undergo, they are fit to undergo through some power that moves and compels them from outside. It remains, then, that ensouled things have this appearance, and are self-moving in a second way, while the soul in them moves itself and is moved by itself first; and that, by a power from itself, as it gives life to bodies, so it also extends to them from itself an appearance of being moved by themselves.

flags.taylor: rightly following Socrates, and considering what the end of things is
flags.why: Proclus seems to mean Socrates in the Phaedrus (245c-e), who proves the soul immortal as the self-moving source of motion; Taylor's "the end of things" is unclear, and may mean "the result", what follows.

paragraphs.modern: If, then, self-moving being is older than the natures moved by others, and soul is first of all self-moving, giving bodies an image of self-motion, soul will be above bodies, and the motion of every body will be the offspring of soul and of the motion in it. So the whole heaven, and all the bodies in it, having various motions and moved with these different motions by nature (for circling is natural to every such body), must have ruling souls, older in being than bodies, moved in themselves, and lighting up the bodies from above with the power of being moved. These souls, which set in order the whole world and its parts and give to every body, lifeless in itself, the power of being moved, breathing into it the cause of motion for this, must move all things either by reason or in the opposite way, which it is not lawful to say. If this world, and everything in it that is set in order and moves evenly and for ever by nature, as is proved partly in the mathematical studies and partly in the study of nature, hung from an irrational soul, which moves itself and others, then neither the order of the circuits, nor the motion bounded by one reason, nor the position of the bodies, nor anything else that comes about by nature, would have a stable cause, able to set out everything in order and always in the same way. For everything irrational is by nature fit to be ordered by something other than itself, and is unlimited and unordered in its own nature. To hand over the whole heaven, and a circuit turning by reason and always the same, to such a thing fits neither the nature of things nor our untaught ideas. But if an intellectual soul, which uses reason, governs all things, and if everything moved in an everlasting motion is governed by such a soul, and none of the wholes in the universe lacks soul (for "no body is honourable without such a power", as Theophrastus says somewhere), then does this soul have its intellectual, perfect and beneficent power by sharing, or by its very being? If by its being, then every soul must be of this kind, since each is self-moving by its own nature. But if by sharing, there will be another intellect, actual and older than soul, which has thinking in its very being and, by its very being, holds first in itself the one-like knowledge of all things. For the soul whose being is defined by reason must have what belongs to intellect by sharing, and the intellectual nature must be twofold: one first, in divine intellect itself; the other proceeding from it, second, in soul. You may add to these, if you like, the presence of intellectual light in body. For how is this whole heaven spherical, or moved in a circle? How does it turn with the same circuit in one fixed order? How could it always keep the same Form and power, unchanged, by nature, if it did not share in being formed by intellect? For soul supplies motion. But the cause of firm stability, which brings the unsteady change of moving things back to sameness, and of a life bounded by one reason and a circuit always the same, will clearly be above soul.

flags.taylor: possess this intellectual, perfect, and beneficent power, according to participation, or according to essence
flags.why: That is, whether the world-soul is intelligent by its very being (so that every soul would be), or by sharing in an intellect above it. Proclus takes the second: intellect is above soul.

notes: Laws X 896e-898c: the soul that drives the heaven must be the best soul, using intellect, since the heaven moves uniformly in a circle, as intellect does. Theophrastus' words come from a lost work.

paragraphs.modern: So body, and the whole of this perceptible nature, belongs among the things moved by another. Soul moves itself, and binds all bodily motions in itself. And before soul is intellect, which is unmoved. But let no one think that I mean this stillness of intellect to be like something sluggish, lifeless and without breath. It is the leading cause of all motion, and the source, if you like to call it so, of all life: of the life that turns back to itself and of the life that has its existence in other things. Through these causes, too, Timaeus calls the world a living being with soul and intellect. He calls it a living being by its own nature and by the life that reaches it from soul and is spread about it; ensouled, by the presence of a divine soul in it; and with intellect, by the rule of intellect. For the supply of life, the government of soul and the sharing in intellect hold together and contain the whole heaven.
notes: Timaeus 30b: the world came to be "a living being, ensouled and with intellect". Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated ("without breath").

paragraphs.modern: But this intellect is intellect by its very being, since Timaeus, pointing out that the being of intellect is the same as its thinking, calls it divine: he says that soul, taking hold of a divine intellect, led a straight and wise life. If this is so, the whole world must hang from its divinity. Motion must come to this universe from soul; its everlasting remaining and sameness from intellect; and its one union, the breathing together and sympathy in it, and its complete measure, from that unity by which intellect is one-like, soul is one, every being is whole and perfect in its own nature, and every second thing, besides its perfection in its own nature, shares in another, higher character from an order always set above it. For what is bodily, moved by another, gets from soul the appearance of self-moving power, and through soul is a living being. Soul, which moves itself, shares in a life by intellect, and though it acts in time it has an unceasing activity and an ever-wakeful life from its nearness to intellect. And intellect, having its life in eternity, always actual in its very being, and fixing all its stable thinking at once in itself, is wholly made divine through the cause before it. For it has two kinds of activity, as Plotinus says: some as intellect, and others as drunk with nectar. And elsewhere he says that this intellect, by what is before it and is not intellect, is a god, just as soul, by its summit, which is above soul, is intellect, and body, by the power before body, is soul.
notes: "Taking hold of a divine intellect": the Laws (897b), of the soul that governs the heaven. Plotinus VI.7.35: intellect has one power for thinking and another, "drunk with nectar", by which it sees what is beyond it. Taylor's three footnotes correct the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: So all things, as we have said, hang from the One, through intellect and soul as middles. Intellect has the form of the One; soul has the form of intellect; and the body of the world is alive. Everything is joined to what is before it. Of the natures after these, one enjoys the divine more nearly and another more distantly. Divinity is before intellect, carried first in an intellectual nature. Intellect is most divine, as made divine before the others. Soul is divine so far as it needs intellect as a middle. And the body that shares in such a soul is itself divine as body, since the light of the divine reaches from above even to the last things that hang from it. Yet it is not simply divine. Soul, by looking to intellect and living from itself, is divine first.

flags.taylor: but soul, by looking to intellect, and living from itself, is primarily divine
flags.why: This seems to contradict what was just said, that divinity is first in intellect. Proclus means that soul is the first of the things that are divine by sharing, before body, while intellect is divine by its very being; Taylor's footnote supplies the word "divine" earlier in the paragraph.

paragraphs.modern: My argument is the same about each of the whole spheres and the bodies they hold. All these imitate the whole heaven, since they too have an everlasting lot. As for the elements below the moon, they do not wholly change in their being: they remain in the universe as wholes, and hold in themselves partial living beings. For every whole has after it more partial beings. As in the heavens the number of the stars proceeds together with the whole spheres, and on earth the multitude of partial earthly animals exists together with their whole, so, I think, in the wholes in between each element must be filled with fitting numbers. For how could the wholes that exist before parts be ranked together with parts in the extremes, unless they have the same proportion in the natures between?
notes: "The wholes in between" are water and air, between the heaven and the earth; their "numbers" are the living beings proper to them (daemons, in Proclus' reading of Timaeus 40a and Epinomis 984b-985b).

paragraphs.modern: If each of the spheres is a living being, always the same, and completes the universe, then, as having life, it will always share first in soul; as keeping its own order in the world unchanged, it will be held by intellect; and as one and a whole, the leader and ruler of its own parts, it will be lit by divine union. So not only the universe but each of its everlasting parts has soul and intellect, and is, as far as possible, like the universe. For each of these parts is a universe in relation to the multitude akin to it. In short, there is one bodily whole of the universe, and many others below it, depending on this one. There is one soul of the universe, and after it other souls which, together with it, set in order the whole parts of the universe with undefiled purity. There is one intellect, and an intellectual number below it, shared by these souls. And there is one god who holds together at once all natures in the world and above the world, and a multitude of other gods, who give out intellectual beings, the souls that hang from them, and all the parts of the world. For we must not suppose that each work of nature generates things like itself, but that the wholes and the first of the beings in the world do not much more hold in themselves the pattern of such a generation. For the like is more akin to the nature of a cause than the unlike, as the same is more than the different, and limit more than the unlimited. These things, however, we will study exactly later on. Now we will turn to the second of the things proved in the Laws, that the gods take care of wholes and parts at once, and briefly discuss Plato's faultless idea of the providence of the gods.
notes: Taylor's footnotes: the Greek he translated must be corrected to read "and like the universe in power", as Portus' Latin has it; and the word "above the world" is supplied.

paragraphs.modern: From what has been said, then, it is clear to everyone that the gods are the causes of all motion. Some of them are of the order of being and life-giving, by a power that moves itself, lives of itself and acts of itself. Others are intellectual: by their very being they rouse all second natures to perfection of life, as the source and principle of all second and third processions of motion. Others are unitary, having the character of the One. These make divine, by sharing, all the whole kinds below them, by a first, complete and unknowable power of activity, and they lead one kind of motion without being the principle of another. Others again give second natures motion in place or in quality, but are the causes of motion to themselves by their very being. For everything that causes being in others is, far before this, the cause to itself of its own activities and perfection. Further, what moves itself is again the principle of motion: being and life are given by soul to everything in the world, and not motion in place only and the other kinds of motion, but the coming forth into being comes from soul, and far before that from intellectual being, which binds to itself the life of self-moving natures and goes before every activity in time as its cause. And still more do motion, being and life proceed from a unitary hyparxis, which holds together intellect and soul, is the source of all good, and proceeds to the last of things. Not all the parts of the world can share in life, nor in intellect and the power of knowing; but all things share in the One, down to matter itself: wholes and parts, things according to nature and things against it. Nothing lacks a cause of this kind, and nothing could ever share in being if it lacked the One. If, then, the gods produce all things and hold all things in their own unknowable embrace, how could there not be in that embrace a providence of all things, reaching from above to the most partial natures? Everywhere it is fitting that offspring should enjoy the care of their causes. All things moved by another are offspring of self-moving natures. Things in time, whether in the whole of time or in part of it, are effects of eternal natures, since what always is is the cause of what sometimes is. And the divine and unitary kinds, as they give existence to all multiplied natures, come before them. In short, there is no being and no multitude of powers that does not have its birth from the One. So all these must share in the providence of the causes before them: given life by the gods of the order of soul, and moving round in periods of time; sharing in sameness and in the stable state of Forms from the intellectual gods; and receiving into themselves the presence of union, of measure and of the giving out of good from the first gods. So either the gods know that caring for their own offspring is natural to them, and do not only give existence to second beings and supply them with life, being and union, but also hold first in themselves the first cause of the goods these beings have; or else, which it is not lawful to say, though they are gods they do not know what is proper and fitting.
notes: Laws X 899b: the gods are the souls (and intellects) that cause the motions of the heaven, so "all things are full of gods" (Thales' saying). Taylor's footnotes correct the Greek he translated and supply "from the intellectual gods".

paragraphs.modern: For how can those who are the causes of beauty be ignorant of beautiful things, or those whose hyparxis is defined by the nature of the good be ignorant of good things? If they are ignorant, then souls do not govern the universe by intellect, nor are intellects carried in souls as in a vehicle, nor, before these, do the henads of the gods hold all knowledge drawn together in themselves, as we granted through the earlier proofs. If, then, they do not lack knowledge, being the fathers, leaders and governors of everything in the world, and the care of what they govern, of what follows them and what they produce belongs to them as such, shall we say that they know the law of nature and fulfil it, or that through weakness they fail to care for their possessions or offspring? (It makes no difference to the present argument which of these two names you choose.) If they neglect the care of wholes for lack of power, what is the cause of this lack? For they do not move things from outside, while other things are the causes of being. They take charge of the things they have produced, and they rule over all things as from the stern of a ship, themselves supplying being, themselves holding the measures of life, and themselves giving out to things their activities.
notes: Laws X 902b-903a: since all things are the possessions of the gods, and the gods are the best of masters, they cannot neglect them. "As from the stern of a ship": Statesman 272e, of the god who steers the universe, and Critias 109c.

paragraphs.modern: Are they, then, unable to provide for all things at once, or do they leave none of the parts without their care? And if they do not care for everything in the world, do they look after greater things and neglect the smaller, or attend to the smaller and neglect the greater? If we deny them care of all things alike through lack of power, how can we grant them the greater thing, the making of all things, and refuse them what follows naturally from it, care for what they have made? For it belongs to the power that produces the greater to arrange the smaller well. But if they care for the smaller and neglect the greater, how can this kind of providence be right? For what is more akin and more like a thing is fitted by nature to share more properly in the good it gives. If, again, the gods think the first of the natures in the world worthy of their care, and of the perfection of which they are the sources, but cannot reach to the last of things, what can keep the presence of the gods from reaching all things? What can hinder their ungrudging and overflowing activity? How can those able to do greater things be unable to govern lesser ones? Or how can those who produce the being even of the smallest things not be masters of their perfection, through lack of power? All these things are hostile to our natural ideas. It remains, then, that the gods know what is fitting and proper, and that they have a power suited to the perfection of their own nature and to the government of all things. But if they know what is according to nature, and for the generating causes of all things this is to care for all things, and they have an overflowing power, then they are not without this kind of care. Together with what has been said, is there also in them the will to provide? Or is this alone missing from their knowledge and power, so that things are left without their care? For if, knowing what is fitting for them and able to do what they know, they are unwilling to provide for their own offspring, they will lack goodness, their ungrudging overflowing will perish, and we will be doing nothing else than doing away with the hyparxis that is their very being. For the very being of the gods is defined by the good, and they exist in it. To provide for what is below is to give it some good. How, then, can we take providence from the gods without at the same time taking away their goodness? And if we do away with their goodness, how can we not also, unknowingly, do away with their hyparxis, which we established in the earlier proofs? So we must admit, as following from the very being of the gods, that they are good with every virtue. And again it follows from this that they do not withdraw from caring for second natures, whether through idleness, weakness or ignorance. And from this, I think, it follows too that in them are the best knowledge, undefiled power, and an ungrudging and overflowing will. From which it appears that they provide for the whole of things and leave out nothing needed for the giving of good.
notes: Laws X 900c-903a: the gods know, can and will care for small things as well as great, as a doctor or a builder cares for the small parts with the whole. Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: But let no one think that the gods exercise their providence over second things in a busy or laborious way, or that this is so with their transcendence, set far from mortal toil. For their blessedness will not be soiled by the trouble of administration, since even the life of good men goes easily and is free of annoyance and pain. All labour and annoyance come from the hindrances of matter. If we must define the manner of the gods' providence, we must admit that it is unforced, undefiled, immaterial and inexpressible. For the gods do not govern all things by searching out what is fitting, or exploring the good of each thing by uncertain reasonings, or by looking outside themselves and following their effects, as men do in the care they take of their own affairs. Having in themselves first the measures of all things, producing the being of each thing from themselves, and looking to themselves, they lead and perfect all things on a silent path by their very being, and fill them with good. Nor do they produce as nature does, acting only by their being without choice; nor, acting as partial souls do, with will, do they lack production by their being. They draw both together into one union. They will what they can do by their very being; and, able by their very being to produce all things, they hold the cause of production in their ungrudging and overflowing will. With what busy activity, then, with what trouble, or with the punishment of what Ixion, is the providence of the whole souls, or of intellectual beings, or of the gods themselves carried out, unless someone says that to give good in any way is laborious to the gods? But nothing is laborious to anything that is according to its nature. It is not laborious for fire to give heat, or for snow to cool, or, in short, for bodies to act by their own powers. Before bodies, it is not laborious for natures to nourish, generate or increase, for these are the works of natures. Nor, again, before these, is it laborious for souls. They produce many activities by choice, many by their very being, and are the causes of many motions merely by being present. So if giving good is according to nature for the gods, providence too is according to nature. And we must say that these things are done by the gods with ease, and by their very being alone. But if these things are not according to nature, the gods will not be good by nature either. For the good supplies good, as life is the source of other life and intellect of intellectual light. And everything that is first in each nature generates what is second in it.

flags.taylor: with the punishment of what Ixion
flags.why: Ixion was bound for ever to a turning wheel; Proclus means a providence that would be endless forced labour, like his.

notes: "On a silent path": the Trojan Women of Euripides (887-888), of Zeus who "leads all mortal things by justice on a silent path". Aristotle, On the Heavens II.1 (284a), also says that the heaven's motion would be laborious if it were forced, like Ixion's wheel.

paragraphs.modern: But what I would call the glorious distinction of Plato's theology is this. By it, the set-apart being of the gods is not turned towards second natures through caring for what is below; nor is their providential presence to all things lessened by their being above the whole of things in undefiled purity. Plato's theology gives them, at the same time, a separate existence, unmixed with every lower nature, and also a reach to all things, and the care and ordering of their own offspring. The way they pass through all things is not bodily, as light passes through the air; nor divided about bodies, as in nature; nor turned towards lower things, as with a partial soul. It is separate from body and does not turn towards it; it is immaterial, unmixed, unhindered, one-like, first and set apart. In short, this is how we must think of the gods' providence for now. Clearly it will be proper to each order of gods. Soul is said to provide for second natures in one way, and intellect in another. The providence of the divinity before intellect works by a transcendence over both intellect and soul. And among the gods themselves, the providence of the gods below the moon differs from that of the heavenly gods. Of the gods above the world, too, there are many orders, and the manner of providence differs in each.

The third question we will join to the earlier ones, and consider how we are to understand that the gods cannot be turned aside: that they do all things by justice and do not in the least overturn its limit or its straight rule in their care for all other things and in the changes of human affairs. I think it is clear to everyone that whatever rules according to nature, and gives all possible care to the happiness of those it rules, thereby leads what it rules and directs it to what is best. The pilot who rules the sailors and the ship has no other main aim than the safety of those who sail in it and of the ship itself. The doctor who has charge of the sick does everything for nothing else than the health of those in his care, whether he must cut them or give them a purge. Nor would a general or a guardian say they look to any other end than, one, the freedom of those he guards, and the other, of his soldiers. Nor will anyone else whose task is to lead or take care of others try to overturn the good of those who follow him, which it is his business to bring about, and with a view to which he arranges everything for those he governs. If, then, we grant that the gods are the leaders of the whole of things, and that their providence reaches all things, since they are good and have every virtue, how can they neglect the happiness of those in their care? Or how can they be worse than other leaders in their care for lower natures? For the gods always look to what is better, and set this as the end of all their government, while other leaders overlook the good of men and embrace vice rather than virtue, when they are corrupted by the gifts of the wicked.
notes: Laws X 905d-907b: the gods are like pilots, charioteers, generals, doctors, farmers and shepherds, and none of these would betray those in their charge for gifts.

paragraphs.modern: In general, whether you choose to call the gods leaders, rulers, guardians or fathers, the divine nature will be seen to lack none of these names. For everything holy and honourable is in them first. And this is why here too some things are by nature more holy and honourable than others: they show the last likeness of the gods. But why say more on this? For I think we hear those wise in divine things praise fatherly, guarding, ruling and healing powers. How, then, can the images of the gods that exist by nature, looking to the end suited to them, care for the order of the things they govern, while the gods themselves, with whom are the whole of good, true and real virtue and a blameless life, would not direct their government to the virtue and vice of men? And how, on this view, could we admit that they show virtue victorious in the universe and vice defeated? Would they not then corrupt the measures of justice through the worship paid them by the wicked, overturn the limit of unswerving knowledge, and make the gifts of vice appear more honourable than the pursuits of virtue? This kind of providence is good neither for these leaders nor for those who follow them. For those who have become wicked there will be no release from guilt, since they will always try to get ahead of justice and bend the measures of what is due. And it would follow, which it is not lawful to say, that the gods aim at the vice of those in their care, neglect their true safety, and so are the causes only of a shadow of good. This universe, too, and the whole world will be filled with disorder and incurable confusion, vice remaining in it, full of the discord found in badly governed cities. And is it not wholly impossible that parts should be governed according to nature more than wholes, human things more than divine, and images more than first causes?

flags.taylor: paternal, guardian, ruling and pæonian powers
flags.why: "Paeonian" means healing, from Paeon, the healer of the gods, a name of Apollo. Those "wise in divine things" are the theologians, the Orphics and the Chaldean Oracles, which name such orders of gods.

flags.taylor: consequently be alone the causes of adumbrant good
flags.why: Taylor's "adumbrant" means shadowy: a good in appearance only.

paragraphs.modern: So if men rightly look after the welfare of men in governing them, honouring some and disgracing others, and everywhere correcting the works of vice by the measures of virtue, much more must the gods be the unswerving governors of the whole of things. For men get this virtue by being like the gods. But if we grant that men who corrupt the safety and well-being of those they govern imitate the gods' providence more, we will unknowingly overturn at one and the same time the truth about the gods and the high worth of virtue. For this, I think, is clear to everyone: what is more like the gods is happier than what is cut off from them by unlikeness and difference. So if among men the uncorrupted and unswerving form of providence is honourable, it must surely be much more honourable among the gods. But if among them mortal gifts were more holy than the divine measures of justice, then among men too earthly gifts would be more honourable than Olympian goods, and the flatteries of vice than the works of virtue. With a view, then, to the most perfect happiness, Plato in the Laws gives us through these proofs the hyparxis of the gods, their care reaching to all things, and their unchanging activity. These are common to all the gods, but are first and chief by nature in the teaching about them. For this triad seems to reach as far as the most partial natures in the divine orders, starting from above, from the hidden kinds of gods. For a one-like hyparxis, a power that cares for all second natures, and an unswerving and unchanging intellect are in all the gods, both before the world and in it.
notes: "Earthly gifts" and "Olympian goods": the Laws (V 727e-728a) sets the goods of the soul above gold "on earth or under it". Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Again, from another starting point we can grasp the proofs of theology in the Republic. These are common to all the divine orders, reach alike through the whole discussion of the gods, and unfold the truth for us in unbroken connection with what has been said. In the second book of the Republic Socrates sets out certain patterns of theology for the poets who make myths, and urges his pupils to clean themselves of the tragic teachings that some do not refuse to bring to the divine nature, hiding in them, as in veils, the secret mysteries about the gods. As I said, Socrates sets out the patterns and laws of myths about the gods, which give both this outward meaning and the inner hidden aim, which looks to the beautiful and the natural in the inventions about the gods. First he sees fit to show, by our unspoiled idea of the gods and their goodness, that they supply all good but are never the cause of any evil to any being. Second, he says that they are unchanging in their being, that they do not take on various shapes to deceive and bewitch, and are not the authors of the greatest evil, lying in deed or word, or of error and folly. These, then, are two laws, and the first has two conclusions: that the gods are not the causes of evils, and that they are the causes of all good. The second law likewise has two other conclusions: that every divine nature is unchanging, and that it is set pure of falsehood and contrived variety. So all that is proved depends on these three common ideas about the divine nature: its goodness, its unchangeableness and its truth. For the first and inexpressible source of good is with the gods; together with eternity, the cause of a power that is always the same; and the first intellect, which is the beings themselves, and the truth that is in real beings.
notes: Republic II 379a-383c: the first law (380c), "god is not the cause of all things, but of the good"; the second (383a), the gods are not wizards who change their shape, nor do they mislead us by lies in word or deed.

paragraphs.modern: What has its hyparxis and its whole being defined in the good, and produces all things by its very being, must produce every good and no evil. If there were something good first that was not god, perhaps one could say that the divine is a cause of good, but does not give every good to beings. But not only is every god good: what is first of all good in form and beneficent is god. For what is good first will not come second after the gods, since everywhere what is second receives the character of its hyparxis from what is first. So it is wholly necessary that the divine be the cause of good, and of all the goods that proceed in the second descents, down to the last of things. For as the power that causes life gives existence to all life, the power that causes knowledge produces all knowledge, and the power that causes beauty produces everything beautiful, the beauty in words and the beauty in what appears; and as every first cause produces from itself everything like it and binds to itself the one reality of the things that exist by one form, so, I think, the first and chief good, the one-like hyparxis, establishes in and about itself the causes and embraces of all goods at once. There is nothing good that does not have this power from it, nothing beneficent that does not share in this cause by turning back to it. For all goods are produced, perfected and kept from there, and the one series and order of all good depends on that source. Through the same cause of hyparxis, then, the gods supply all good and no evil. What is first of all good gives existence to every good from itself, and is not the cause of a lot contrary to itself; since what produces life is not the cause of the loss of life, and the source of beauty is set apart from the nature of what lacks beauty and is ugly, and from its causes. So of what first establishes the good it is not lawful to say that it is the cause of contrary offspring; the nature of goods proceeds from it undefiled, unmixed and one-like.

flags.taylor: for that which is primarily good will not be the second after the Gods
flags.why: The point is that nothing can be good first and yet below the gods: whatever is good first is itself divine, so the gods are the causes of all good.

paragraphs.modern: The divine cause of goods is set eternally in itself, and gives all second natures an ungrudging and overflowing share of good. Of those that share, some keep their share with incorruptible purity, receiving their proper good in undefiled embraces, and so, through an abundance of power, have without fail a lot of goods suited to them. But the natures set at the last of the whole of things also enjoy, by their nature, the goodness of the gods, for what wholly lacks good could not be or come to be at all. Yet when they receive such an outflow, they do not keep the gift that reaches them pure and unmixed, nor hold their own good steadily and always the same. Becoming weak, partial and material, and filled with the lack of life of what underlies them, they show disorder in place of order, unreason in place of reason, and vice, the contrary of virtue, in place of virtue. The natures ranked as wholes are each set free of this kind of perversion, since what is more perfect in them always rules by nature. But partial natures, through a lessening of power, always turning aside into multitude, division and extension, darken their share of good and put its contrary in its place, mixed with the good and overcome in the mixture. For here too it is not lawful for evil to exist unmixed and wholly without good. Though a thing may be evil to a part, it is wholly good to the whole and to the universe. For the universe is always happy, and is always made of perfect parts that are according to nature. But what is against nature is always evil to partial natures, and in these are ugliness, lack of proportion, perversion and an appearance of existence. What is destroyed is destroyed to itself, and falls away from its proper perfection, but to the universe it is incorruptible and indestructible.
notes: Taylor's footnotes correct two words of the Greek he translated ("wholes" for "others").

paragraphs.modern: Everything that lacks good, so far as concerns itself and its own existence, lacks it through weakness of nature; but it is good to the whole, so far as it is a part of the universe. For no lack of life, no ugliness or lack of measure, no privation at all can be put into the universe. Its whole number is always perfect, held together by the goodness of wholes. Life is present everywhere, together with existing and being perfect, so far as each thing completes the whole. So the divine, as we have said, is the cause of good; but the shadowy existence of evil comes not from power but from the weakness of the natures that receive the gods' light. Nor is evil in wholes, but in partial natures, and not in all of these. For the first of partial natures and the partial intellectual kinds have the form of the good eternally. But those in the middle among them, which act in time and join their share in the good to change and motion in time, cannot keep the gift of the gods unmoved, one-like and simple: by their variety they darken its simplicity, by their many forms its oneness of form, and by their mixture its purity and incorruptibility. For they are not made of incorruptible first kinds, nor do they have a simple being or one-like powers, but powers made of the contraries of these, as Socrates says somewhere in the Phaedrus. And the last of partial natures, which are also material, much more pervert their own good. They are mixed with lack of life and have an existence like an image's, full of much non-being, made of things hostile to each other and of circumstances that change and are scattered through the whole of time. So they never stop showing in everything that they are given over to corruption, lack of proportion, ugliness and all kinds of change. They are not only extended in their activities, like the natures before them, but are full, in their powers and activities, of what is against nature and of the weakness of matter. For things that come to be in a foreign place, bringing in the whole together with form, rule over the underlying nature; but falling back again from their proper whole into the partial, and sharing in divisibility, weakness, war and the division that is the source of becoming, they must change in every way. So not every being is wholly good, or there would be no destruction and generation of bodies, nor purification and punishment of souls. Nor is there any evil in wholes, or the world would not be a blessed god, if the chief parts it is made of were imperfect. Nor are the gods the causes of evils as they are of goods. Evil comes from the weakness of what receives good, and from being set at the last of things. Nor is the evil that has a shadowy existence in partial natures unmixed with good. It shares in good in a way, being held in existence by good. In short, evil that wholly lacks all good cannot exist. For evil itself is beyond even what in no way exists, just as the Good itself is beyond what wholly is. Nor is the evil in partial natures left in disorder: even this is made to serve good ends by the gods, and for this reason justice cleans souls of vice, and another order of gods cleans away the vice in bodies. All things, though, are turned as far as possible to the goodness of the gods. The wholes remain within their own limits, and so do the perfect and beneficent kinds of beings. But the more partial and imperfect natures are ordered and arranged as is fitting, serve the completing of wholes, are called up to the beautiful, are changed, and in every way enjoy their share in the good, as far as they can.

flags.taylor: For evil itself is even beyond that which in no respect whatever has an existence
flags.why: Proclus means that evil "itself", evil without any good, would be even less than nothing; so it cannot exist, as the Good is above what wholly is. Taylor's footnotes supply "cause" and correct "darken" in the Greek he translated.

notes: The Phaedrus (246a-b): the souls of gods have horses and charioteers all good and of good stock, but in other souls they are mixed. "The world a blessed god": Timaeus 34b.

paragraphs.modern: For there can be no greater good for each of these than what the gods give to their offspring by measure. All things, each one apart and all in common, receive as much good as they can share in. If some are filled with greater goods and others with lesser, the cause must be put down to the power of what receives and to the measures of the giving. Different things suit different beings by their nature. But the gods always hold out good, as the sun always sends out light. Each thing receives this light differently, by its rank, and receives the largest share of light it can. All things are led by justice, and good is absent from nothing, but present to everything, by the proper limit of its share. And, as the Athenian Stranger says, all things are in a good state and set in order by the gods. So let no one say that there are original forming principles of evil in nature, or intellectual patterns of evils as there are of goods, or an evil-working soul, or a cause that produces evil among the gods; nor let anyone bring in revolt and eternal war against the first Good. All these are foreign to Plato's science, and, being further from the truth, wander off into barbarian folly and the myths of the giants. And if certain people, speaking darkly in secret stories, devise things of this kind, we will make no change in the outward dress of what they point to. But we must search out the truth of those things, and meanwhile receive Plato's science purely into the pure embraces of the soul, and keep it undefiled and unmixed with contrary opinions.

flags.taylor: there are precedaneous productive principles of evil in nature
flags.why: Taylor's "precedaneous" (going before, original) and "productive principles" (logoi): Proclus denies that evil has forming principles in nature or patterns in intellect, against those, like the Gnostics and the Manichaeans, or a reading of the Laws' "evil soul" (896e), who posit a cause of evil.

notes: Laws X 903b-904a: all things are ordered by the one who cares for the whole, with a view to the preservation and excellence of the whole. "The myths of the giants": the war of the giants against the gods (Sophist 246a, Republic 378c). "Barbarian folly" seems to point to the Persian teaching of two opposed principles.

Many admonitions that the supercelestial place is triadic. And what the signs are of the three hypostases in it.
Who Adrastia is. What the sacred law of Adrastia is. That she ranks in the supercelestial place. And on what account she does so.
A summary account of what is said about the supercelestial place, unfolding the peculiarities of it.
Demonstrations that the connectedly-containing order is in the intelligible and intellectual Gods. And that it is necessary there should be three connective causes of wholes.
That according to Plato the celestial circulation is the same with the connective order.
How we may obtain auxiliaries from what is said by Plato of the triadic division in the connective deity. And why he especially venerates the union in this triad.
What the theology in the Cratylus is concerning Heaven. And how it is possible to collect from it by a reasoning process the middle of the intelligible and intellectual Gods.
That the most divinely-inspired of the interpreters have defined the subcelestial arch to be a certain peculiar order. And that our preceptor has unfolded it in the most perfect manner.
Many admonitions that the peculiarity of the subcelestial arch is perfective, from what Plato has delivered concerning it, and from the souls that are elevated to it.
What the triadic division is of the perfective order, which Plato has delivered in the subcelestial arch.

What the elevation is of souls separate from bodies to the intelligible and intellectual triads. What the most blessed telete is. What muesis, and epopteia are. What the entire, simple, and unmoved visions are. And what the end is of all this elevation.
How Plato unfolds in the Parmenides, from intelligibles the intelligible and intellectual orders. And what that which is common, and that which is different are, in the theology concerning these.
How the intelligible and intellectual number proceeds from intelligibles. And in what it differs from intelligible multitude.
How divine number adorns all beings. And what the powers in it are which are symbolically delivered from the division of number.
How Parmenides has delivered the feminine and generative peculiarity [of first number] in what he says concerning number.
How we may discover in what is delivered concerning number, the triadic division of the summit of intelligibles and intellectuals.
Whether it is proper to place number prior to animal itself, or in animal itself, or posterior to it.
Whence Parmenides begins to speak about number. How far he proceeds in what he says about it. And how he unfolds the different orders in it.
What the unknown is in divine numbers. What the generative is in them. And admonitions of these things from what is elsewhere said by Plato concerning numbers.
How Parmenides delivers the middle order of intelligibles and intellectuals through the one, whole, and finite. And what the peculiarities are of these.

Whence Parmenides begins to speak about this order. And how far he proceeds in what he says about it. How he likewise unfolds the three monads in it conformably to what is said in the Phædrus concerning them.
How Parmenides delivers the third order of intelligibles and intellectuals. And how he unfolds the perfective peculiarity, and triadic division of it.
An admonition what the union is of the three intelligible and intellectual triads, from the conclusions of Parmenides.
How many theological dogmas we may assume, through the order of the conclusions delivered by Parmenides in his discourse concerning the intelligible and intellectual Gods.
How the intellectual orders proceed from the intelligible and intellectual Gods. And according to what peculiarities they subsist.
What the division is of the intellectual Gods. And the progression according to hebdomads in this order of Gods.
Who the three intellectual fathers are according to Plato. What the three undefiled monads are. And who the seventh deity is, that is co-arranged with the two triads.
How from the writings of Plato, the procession of the intellectual Gods into seven hebdomads may be collected by a reasoning process.

Who the mighty Saturn is, according to the theology in the Cratylus. And how he is in a certain respect intelligible, and in a certain respect intellectual. In which also, the dogmas are discussed concerning the union of intellect with the intelligible, and its separation from it.
What the kingdom of Saturn is. In what manner it is delivered by Plato in the Politicus. And of what it is the cause to the world, to the mundane Gods, and to partial souls.
What the Saturnian life of souls is. And what peculiarities of this circulation the Elean Guest delivers.
How souls are said to be nourished by intelligibles. And what the difference is of the nutriment derived from different intelligibles.
What the orders are which the mighty Saturn causes to preside over wholes. In which also, who the Saturnian intellect is that is delivered in the Gorgias is unfolded.
How this God [Saturn] is peculiarly called by theologists insenescible, or free from old age. And how Plato has delivered this peculiarity of him.
Who the vivific Goddess is. How she is the collector of the Saturnian and Jovian kingdoms. And what orders she possesses conjoined with both these kingdoms.
Who the third father in intellectuals is. How he proceeds from the causes prior to him. And that he is the demiurgus of the universe.
Demonstrations that the whole demiurgus of the universe, is the third father of the intellectual Gods.

An answer to those who say that there are three demiurgi according to Plato, demonstrating through many arguments that the demiurgic monad is arranged prior to the [demiurgic] triad, in the third order of intellectuals.
That Timæus especially delivers the peculiarity of the demiurgus, by calling him intellect. And that this pertains to the third of the intellectual fathers.

How according to another method it is requisite to discover the peculiarity of the demiurgus. And how the demiurgus is called in the Timæus effector and father. In which also, it is clearly shown, where the paternal, where the paternal and at the same time effective, where the effective and paternal, and where the effective only are, according to Plato. And in short, in what effector and father differ.
How following Timæus, according to a third method, we may purify our conceptions concerning the demiurgic monad.
A theological explanation of the speech of the demiurgus in the Timæus, distinctly evolving our conceptions about the demiurgic energy.
What the second speech of the demiurgus is to divisible souls. In what it differs from the former. And how in this all the measures of the life of souls are defined.
A summary of all that is said about the demiurgus, following the doctrine of Timæus.
Admonitions from what is said in the Cratylus, that Plato attributes fabrication to Jupiter.
Admonitions from what is said in the Cratylus of the fabrication of Jupiter. In which also the concord is demonstrated of the theology from names, with the arrangement of the demiurgus in the Timæus.
Admonitions of the fabrication of Jupiter from what is demonstrated in the Philebus. In which also it is shown, what the royal soul, and the royal intellect are.
Demonstrations of the same thing, from what is said in the Protagoras about the political science.
An argument shewing that Jupiter is the demiurgus and father of the universe according to Plato, from what is said in the Politicus concerning the twofold circulation [of the universe.]
How Jupiter subsists according to cause in animal itself, and how animal itself is in Jupiter.
How Timæus attributes to the demiurgus the unknown and ineffable.
Why Timæus thinks fit to denominate animal itself, and is of opinion that it may be known, but leaves the demiurgus unknown and ineffable.
Concerning the Crater in the Timæus, a theology teaching what the genera are that are mingled in it, and how it is the cause of the essence of souls.
That the Crater in the Timæus is fontal. And admonitions from the writings of Plato, concerning the principle and fountain of souls.
That the three vivific fountains co-arranged with the demiurgus, may be assumed from what is said in the Timæus, viz. the fountain of souls, the fountain of the virtues, and the fountain of natures.
Admonitions concerning the undefiled Gods; that there are such Gods according to Plato; and what the peculiarity is of their essence.
More manifest demonstrations of the hypostasis of the undefiled Gods, according to Plato.

Admonitions through many arguments how it is proper to denominate the undefiled Gods according to Plato. In which also, the union of them, what their separation, and what their peculiarity are, is delivered.
How from what is mystically asserted by Plato, auxiliaries may be obtained, concerning the seventh monad of intellectuals.
How Plato delivers in the Parmenides the summit of the intellectual Gods.
How Parmenides unfolds the middle order of the intellectual breadth, and through what signs.
How Parmenides defines the third order of intellectuals, and through what peculiarities.

That the ruling order of Gods is in continuity with the intellectual Gods. And that the division into fountains and principles may be assumed from the writings of Plato, through the theory about souls.
How the ruling Gods proceed. And that the supermundane peculiarity pertains to these Gods alone.

What the peculiarity is of the ruling Gods. That the assimilative is especially characteristic of them. And how the causes of assimilation are antecedently assumed in the demiurgus; and how in the intelligible paradigm.
What the powers are of the assimilative Gods. What their energies. And how many goods are imparted by them to the world, and to all mundane natures.
What the divisions are of the assimilative Gods. And that the greatest part of the discourse about them is concerning the middle orders in them.
Many demonstrations, that both according to Plato and other theologists, there is one demiurgus prior to the three demiurgi.
That Jupiter is twofold; one indeed, being prior to the three sons of Saturn, [but the other being one of them.] And how the three proceed from Saturn, and the one Jupiter.
That according to Plato also, the demiurgic monad subsists prior to the three sons of Saturn. Demonstrations of this from what is said in the Politicus, and in the Laws.
More manifest admonitions of the same things from what is said in the Gorgias, and in the Cratylus.
What the vivific triad is among the ruling Gods. And whence we may derive auxiliaries from the writings of Plato concerning the union and division of this triad.

What the convertive triad of the ruling Gods is; and what the monad which it contains. In which also, the union of Apollo with the sun is demonstrated; and it is shewn, how from what is said about Apollo we may be led to the theory of the solar orders.
What the undefiled order is of the ruling Gods. And how from the writings of Plato conceptions about it may be obtained.
How Parmenides forms his conclusions about the ruling Gods, in continuity with the demiurgic order. And that he characterizes the whole order of them, through similitude and dissimilitude.
What the supermundane and at the same time mundane genus of Gods is. And how through their own medium they preserve the continuity of the Gods that proceed from the demiurgus.
How the liberated Gods are characterized. And how from their liberated peculiarity they are exempt from the universe, and are co-arranged with the mundane Gods.
What the common powers, and what the common energies are of the liberated Gods, according with the essence that has been delivered of them.
Concerning the twelve leaders or rulers mentioned in the Phædrus, and that they have a liberated order.
Many and clearer demonstrations that the great leader Jupiter, and all the dodecad of leaders, are liberated.
An explanation from precedaneous causes whence the number of the dodecad in the liberated Gods is derived.
What the division of the liberated leaders is into two monads and one decad. And what the one division of them is.
The theology concerning each of the twelve Gods, unfolding the peculiarities of them from the subjects of their government.

Concerning the mother of the Fates mentioned in the Republic. Likewise concerning the triad of the Fates. What orders they have with reference to each other. What powers of them are delivered through divine symbols. What their energies are. And how Plato characterizes the liberated peculiarity.
How Parmenides forms his conclusions concerning the liberated Gods immediately after the assimilative Gods. And how he characterizes the order of them by touching and not touching.
